jhbl1q2-d1e3503.summary: States the question that will serve as the whole prologue of Book I: whether a wayfarer (viator) cannot perfectly know the pure truth of the Christian faith by the power of human reason alone, without a special divine illumination and the foundation of, and firm adherence to, the Catholic faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e3534.summary: First principal argument against the thesis: drawing on Henry of Ghent (the 'Solemn Doctor', Summa a.1 qq.2, 4, 12), it argues that the intellect, as a natural power, can naturally attain its proper operation of knowing, and that, like sense with respect to every sensible, it is equally ordered from the outset to every knowable truth; so no special illumination is required.
claims: A natural power can naturally attain its natural operation; the intellect is a natural power whose operation is knowing.
As sense is equally apt to know any sensible, the intellect is equally apt to know any intelligible.

jhbl1q2-d1e3559.summary: A second supporting argument within the first principal reason: things with the same ratio of acting are equally apt to act on any receptive subject; since all knowables share one ratio of acting on the intellect, all are equally apt to be known by it.
claims: All intelligible objects act on the intellect by one common ratio and are therefore equally knowable by it.

jhbl1q2-d1e3566.summary: A third supporting argument, modeled on Scotus's first prologue question: since natural reason can perceive common being (ens commune) without special illumination, and whatever can attain a common first object can attain everything contained under it, natural reason can reach any special being, including divine being.
claims: Natural reason attains ens commune without special illumination.
A power that attains a common first object attains whatever falls under it, including divine being.

jhbl1q2-d1e3581.summary: Second principal argument against the thesis: the damned can know the sincere truth of the faith (shown from the rich man in Luke 16), so a wayfarer can know it without special illumination or the foundation of Catholic faith.
claims: The damned, who lack faith and grace, can know the truth of the faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e3593.summary: Supports the second principal argument: a damned heretic could come to know by reason the falsity of his own error even while being punished for it, so a wayfarer can likewise know the truth by reason.
claims: A damned heretic can recognize by reason the falsity of his error.

jhbl1q2-tqdiqf.summary: Further support, taken from Michael of Massa and reported (and answered) by Alphonsus Vargas: demons know the truth of the faith without special illumination, and since the agent and possible intellect are equally disposed in humans and angels (De anima III), the same action follows in a human; hence the question is false.
claims: Demons know the truth of the faith without special illumination.
Where agent and patient are equally proximate, the same action follows; the agent and possible intellects are so disposed in humans as in angels.

jhbl1q2-d1e3643.summary: Third principal argument, set up as a dilemma about how a required special illumination would function: as elevating, as assimilating, both, or not at all. Against elevation: a finite elevation cannot overcome the intellect's indisposition toward an infinite object, while an infinite elevation would exceed even the light of glory, which elevates only finitely; and if the resistance were finite, natural reason could be intensified enough to overcome it.
claims: A finite elevation would be insufficient for an infinite object of faith.
An infinite elevation is impossible since even the light of glory elevates only finitely.

jhbl1q2-d1e3681.summary: A second objection to illumination as elevating: it would elevate either equally with the lights of reason and faith (and so be superfluous) or more than them, in which case the Christian 'sect' would depend more principally on faith than on reason, which the objector takes to be false.
claims: An illumination elevating equally with reason and faith would be superfluous.
It is false that Christian teaching depends more principally on faith than on reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e3688.summary: Gives three reasons for the objector's claim that Christian teaching does not depend more on faith than on reason: assent arises first through evidence, reason confers the nobler mode of being, and the intellect adheres more firmly to reason than to faith.
claims: Assent is first produced through evidence.
The intellect adheres more firmly to rational evidence than to faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e3691.summary: Continues the dilemma: if special illumination elevated more than faith or reason it would amount to scientia and could not coexist with faith, as argued by Gregory of Rimini and Alphonsus (answered by Hugolino and Henry of Ghent). So neither the foundation of faith nor special illumination seems required; the argument then turns to the alternative that illumination works as assimilating.
claims: An illumination more elevating than faith would be scientia, incompatible with faith about the same object.

jhbl1q2-d1e3731.summary: Opens the case against illumination as assimilating: if the assimilating principle were God himself, anyone who had it would seem to be beatified.
claims: If God himself were the assimilating illumination, its possessor would be blessed.

jhbl1q2-d1e3737.summary: Second objection to God as assimilating illumination: everyone so illuminated would have cognition in the Word, even though one could have this assimilation without seeing God.
claims: Identifying the illumination with God would imply that all so illuminated know in the Word.

jhbl1q2-d1e3740.summary: Third objection: on this view, the nearer one came to God the nearer one would come to this assimilation, which the objector takes to be false.
claims: Proximity to God would track degree of assimilating illumination, which is false.

jhbl1q2-d1e3743.summary: Fourth objection: since assimilation works by inherence, identifying it with God would make God inhere in a creature.
claims: Assimilation is by inherence; God cannot inhere in a creature.

jhbl1q2-d1e3746.summary: Fifth objection: since the possible intellect can become all things and God or the Word naturally represents all things, God assimilating the intellect to himself would impress on it all the forms shining in him, and so could not inform it about one thing without many; hence God is not this illumination.
claims: God as assimilating illumination would impress all exemplar forms at once, not one selectively.

jhbl1q2-d1e3749.summary: Closes the dilemma: if the illumination is said to be something other than God, this contradicts the authorities of Hugolino and Henry of Ghent cited earlier.
claims: The proponents of illumination (Hugolino, Henry) do not hold it to be a created thing distinct from God.

jhbl1q2-d1e3764.summary: Fourth principal argument: if the thesis were true, every theologian would receive the special light of illumination; following Alphonsus, and Henry's principle that those who receive it perceive it, modern theologians do not perceive it (they deny it), so they do not have it.
claims: Those who receive the special light perceive it.
Modern theologians deny such a light and so do not perceive or have it.

jhbl1q2-d1e3785.summary: Second supporting argument: theologians can freely dissent from the truths of the faith, since any of them could become a heretic; if they had such a light they would have evidence they could not resist, as one with geometrical evidence cannot dissent from geometry.
claims: Theologians can freely dissent from the faith.
Evident knowledge compels assent and does not allow dissent.

jhbl1q2-d1e3792.summary: Third supporting argument: if theologians had this light, every theologian would assent more firmly to the articles than a simple believer, which is presented as absurd.
claims: Special illumination would make theologians' assent firmer than that of simple believers.

jhbl1q2-d1e3805.summary: Fourth supporting argument: if theologians had such a light, their faith would not be true faith.
claims: Special illumination of theologians would be incompatible with their having faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e3809.summary: Fifth supporting argument, from Thomas of Strasbourg: it is impossible to have such very noble habits and cognitions without their being noticed.
claims: Very noble habits and cognitions cannot remain hidden from their possessor.

jhbl1q2-d1e3822.summary: Sixth supporting argument (unnumbered in the text), by analogy: as one natural light suffices for all natural things, one spiritual light (faith) suffices for all spiritual things, so no additional special illumination is needed.
claims: One spiritual light suffices for all spiritual objects, as one natural light suffices for all natural ones.

jhbl1q2-d1e3826.summary: Seventh supporting argument: if the illumination is, as its defenders say, intermediate between faith and the light of glory, it would have to be so either by negation or by participation, and it is neither.
claims: Special illumination cannot be intermediate between faith and glory by negation or by participation.

jhbl1q2-d1e3836.summary: Fifth principal argument: a wayfarer can prove by human reason that there is a future life after this one, which is one of the articles of the Christian sect; the argument is that, as a stone is naturally inclined to come to rest in some final place, so is man, who is no less ordered to his natural end.
claims: Human reason can demonstrate a future life.
Man is at least as naturally ordered to a final resting place as a stone.

jhbl1q2-d1e3848.summary: Gives a second proof for the fifth argument: everything with sensitive and intellective life acts for an end, and the human good is naturally such as to find rest in something whose attainment brings rest; nothing in this life does so (as Augustine's Confessions affirm), so something beyond this life is required. Reason can therefore reach knowledge of a future life and thus of the truth of the Christian sect.
claims: Nothing in this life gives humans ultimate rest.
Human reason can therefore infer a future life.

jhbl1q2-d1e3900.summary: Adds an authority from Anselm (De conceptu virginali) on the threefold course of things (natural, voluntary, miraculous): if knowledge of the faith's truth were neither natural nor voluntary it would have to be miraculous, which seems unacceptable.
claims: Knowledge of the truth of the faith is not miraculous.

jhbl1q2-d1e3912.summary: A further authority, Hugh of St Victor (De sacramentis I.3): the invisible God becomes known to humans in four ways, two of them by nature. Since the sincere truth of the faith concerns knowledge of the invisible God, it can be had naturally, so the question is false.
claims: Some knowledge of the invisible God is available by nature.

jhbl1q2-d1e3936.summary: Opens the arguments for the opposite (in favor of the thesis) with 1 Corinthians 2 ('we speak wisdom among the perfect') and its gloss that this wisdom cannot be grasped by human reason.
claims: The wisdom of the faith is not comprehensible by human reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e3960.summary: Cites Augustine on Genesis: the authority of Scripture exceeds all the perspicacity of the human race.
claims: Scriptural authority surpasses all human insight.

jhbl1q2-d1e3984.summary: Cites Peter Lombard's prologue, which describes the theological task as an arduous ascent and a work beyond one's powers.
claims: Theology exceeds the natural powers of the inquirer.

jhbl1q2-d1e4012.summary: Cites Augustine (De sermone Domini in monte II): whatever truth the rational soul grasps when it reasons is to be attributed not to the soul but to the light of truth itself.
claims: Truth grasped by reason is due to the divine light of truth, not to the soul.

jhbl1q2-d1e4037.summary: Cites 2 Corinthians 3 ('we are not sufficient of ourselves') for human insufficiency without divine help.
claims: Humans are not sufficient of themselves to think anything as from themselves.

jhbl1q2-d1e4068.summary: Gathers further authorities: 1 Corinthians 12:3 ('no one can say Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit') with Ambrose's gloss that every truth comes from the Holy Spirit, as cited by Henry of Ghent; and Augustine, City of God XI, that canonical Scripture teaches what we must know but cannot know by ourselves.
claims: Every truth, by whomever spoken, is from the Holy Spirit.
There are truths necessary to know that we cannot attain by ourselves.
concepts: Holy Spirit as source of truth

jhbl1q2-d1e4133.summary: Second argument for the opposite, from Augustine (City of God XII): by the efficacy of human reason alone no one can make himself better in any absolute respect, and so no one can become wise by human reason alone.
claims: No one becomes absolutely better or wise by human reason alone.

jhbl1q2-d1e4159.summary: Third argument for the opposite, from Augustine (83 Questions, q.44): no one attains created wisdom unless illuminated by grace, which is God; this is close to a restatement of the question, so the question is true.
claims: Created wisdom is attained only through illumination by God's grace.

jhbl1q2-d1e4193.summary: Fourth argument for the opposite: no one is given to know the sincere truth of the faith without first believing, as Augustine (De utilitate credendi), Richard of St Victor's prologue to De Trinitate, and Augustine on 'Ex ore infantium' teach, as Hugolino also cites; so the question is true.
claims: Belief must precede knowledge of the truth of the faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e4280.summary: Fifth argument for the opposite: without special illumination and the foundation of faith no one can know his own ultimate end perfectly and distinctly, as Scotus argues at length against the philosophers in his first prologue question; since the truth of the faith chiefly concerns that end, the question is true.
claims: Humans cannot know their ultimate end distinctly by natural reason.
The truth of the faith principally concerns the ultimate end.

jhbl1q2-d1e4303.summary: Lays out the plan: this single question will handle the whole prologue in five articles, namely opinions, definitions of terms, conclusions, objections, and replies to the principal arguments and to other objections.

jhbl1q2-d1e4324.summary: Introduces the first article: on this matter there are three kinds of disagreement among those who hold opinions, each with many particular variations.
claims: Opinions on the question fall into three basic disagreements.

jhbl1q2-d1e4334.summary: The first disagreement is among philosophers themselves. Following Henry of Ghent's classification, some put the ratio cognoscendi in something outside the knower. The first such view is Plato's, who placed it in the intelligible archetypal world and an eternal light in which all certain knowledge is had, as reported by Augustine (City of God VIII.7, XII).
claims: Plato located the principle of knowing in an eternal, intelligible light or archetypal world.

jhbl1q2-d1e4403.summary: The second philosophical position is that of Avicenna and the Arabs: unlike Plato they did not have the soul pre-exist, but held that the soul in the body receives habits of knowledge and virtue by influence from a separate intelligence, while bodily obscuring keeps these habits from being actualized.
claims: Avicenna held that habits of knowledge flow from a separate intelligence into the embodied soul.

jhbl1q2-d1e4418.summary: The third philosophical position, attributed to Anaxagoras and Anaximander: all such habits are innate in the soul, not received from outside, and remain latent because the subject is not suitably disposed.
claims: Some held that habits of knowledge are naturally innate and only latent.

jhbl1q2-d1e4428.summary: Opposed to all these is the Peripatetic position, with Aristotle as its head (Augustine, City of God VIII, judging him far inferior to Plato): the ratio cognoscendi lies not in any eternal light or divine art but only in the agent and possible intellect, as in the Posterior Analytics and De anima.
claims: The Peripatetics placed the principle of knowing solely in the agent and possible intellect.

jhbl1q2-d1e4507.summary: Notes that this first disagreement contains many sub-disputes, pointing to Henry of Ghent's account of six ancient errors about the mode of knowing and to a further treatment in a second book (ch. 12).

jhbl1q2-d1e4543.summary: The second disagreement, following Scotus, is between philosophers and Christian doctors: philosophers hold that nature is perfect and deny supernatural influence, while Christian doctors recognize nature's defect and its need for grace, and attribute the perception of truth not only to nature but to divine illumination and grace.
claims: Philosophers deny any need for supernatural influence.
Christian doctors hold that nature is deficient and needs grace for the perception of truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e4565.summary: The third disagreement is among Christian theologians. Some, such as Henry of Ghent and Hugolino, posit an illumination required as a direction of the intellect higher than and distinct from it; others, such as Scotus, Thomas of Strasbourg and Gregory of Rimini, deny it. This ends the first article.
claims: Henry of Ghent and Hugolino hold special illumination necessary; Scotus, Thomas of Strasbourg and Gregory of Rimini deny it.

jhbl1q2-d1e4636.summary: Opens the second article (clarifying terms) with 'truth' (veritas), which is said in three ways. The first is incomplex, as when Christ says 'I am the way, the truth and the life' and Augustine says that the true is that which is.
claims: Truth can be taken incomplexly, as identical with being or with God.

jhbl1q2-d1e4685.summary: The second sense of truth is complex: the total significate of a proposition, the 'complexly signifiable' in the terminology of Gregory of Rimini and Hugolino, a sense Anselm also uses in De veritate.
claims: Truth can be taken as the complexe significabile of a true proposition.

jhbl1q2-d1e4713.summary: The third sense of truth is truth as a sign of truth, as a true proposition is called a truth; in this sense Metaphysics VI says that true and false are in the intellect while good and evil are in things.
claims: A proposition is called a truth as a sign of truth; true and false are in the intellect.

jhbl1q2-d1e4739.summary: Defines the second term, 'Christian sect': the whole congregation of the faithful obediently united under the rite and precepts of their true and principal shepherd, Christ, from whom it is named.
claims: The Christian sect is the congregation of the faithful united under Christ's rite and precepts.

jhbl1q2-d1e4745.summary: Notes that the rite of the sect varies in three ways, as precepts, counsels, and sacraments or ceremonies, and declines to give examples since they are well known.
claims: The Christian rite comprises precepts, counsels and sacraments/ceremonies.

jhbl1q2-d1e4748.summary: Heads off a pejorative reading: 'sect' is not always meant in a bad sense, since the Apostle speaks of 'followers of good works'. Hugh of St Victor is adduced for the view that all ecclesiastical consecration consists in orders, sacred things and precepts.
claims: 'Secta' does not necessarily carry a negative sense.

jhbl1q2-d1e4793.summary: Defines the third term, 'reason' (ratio), which is taken in two ways. First, it is the higher portion of the soul by which man is made in the image and likeness of God (Hugh, De sacramentis; Augustine, De libero arbitrio).
claims: Ratio can denote the higher part of the soul that bears the image of God.

jhbl1q2-d1e4835.summary: Second, ratio is a medium through which the truth or falsity of a previously unknown proposition is made actually known abstractively, as Brinkel defines it. Hiltalingen finds this definition insufficient, because any thing can make another abstractively known.
claims: Brinkel's definition of ratio as a medium of abstractive knowledge is too broad.

jhbl1q2-d1e4865.summary: Acknowledges that this definition seems to agree with Cassiodorus (De anima), who calls reason the soul's power of leading from what is granted and known to the unknown, and with Augustine (De immortalitate animae), who calls it the soul's gaze by which it beholds the true by itself and not through the body.
claims: Reason leads from the known to the unknown.
Reason is the soul's gaze by which it intuits the true without the body.

jhbl1q2-d1e4905.summary: Rejects the definition again, because not everything made known by reason is known abstractively, and proposes his own: reason is that which, by its nature, formally and immediately (not by anyone's imposition), suffices to cause actual knowledge of an otherwise unknown true or false proposition abstractively or deductively. He adds William of St Thierry's (attributed to Bernard) account of reason as the mind's gaze, the contemplation of truth, and rational service, and distinguishes ratiocination (seeking) from reason (finding).
claims: Not everything known by reason is known abstractively.
Reason is what naturally and immediately suffices to cause knowledge of a previously unknown proposition, abstractively or deductively.
Ratiocination seeks; reason finds.

jhbl1q2-d1e4941.summary: Defines the fourth term, 'illumination', which is taken in three ways. First, it is the illuminating principle that assists the mind, as in Augustine's texts (City of God VIII; De libero arbitrio II) where eternal truth is inwardly present and is the light of every mind that discerns unchangeable truths.
claims: Illumination can denote the assisting illuminating principle, the eternal truth present to the mind.

jhbl1q2-d1e4995.summary: Second, illumination is the motion itself by which an illuminated cognitive power is moved to perceive its object vitally.
claims: Illumination can denote the cognitive motion of an illuminated power toward its object.

jhbl1q2-d1e5001.summary: Third, illumination is the act produced or elicited through that motion and through the illumination that assists the illuminated power.
claims: Illumination can denote the cognitive act resulting from illuminative assistance.

jhbl1q2-d1e5011.summary: Defines the fifth term, 'faith', first with Brinkel's definition: a supernaturally infused habit that first elevates the intellect to perceive supernatural truths and by which the faithful wayfarer is first distinguished from the infidel. Hiltalingen leaves its truth and propriety to the reader's judgment.

jhbl1q2-d1e5022.summary: Following Hostiensis's canonistic Summa, begins a list of senses of 'fides'. The first is the sacrament of baptism.
claims: 'Fides' can mean baptism.

jhbl1q2-d1e5044.summary: The second sense of 'fides' is marital chastity (fidelity of the marriage bed), citing Gratian's Decretum.
claims: 'Fides' can mean conjugal fidelity.

jhbl1q2-d1e5050.summary: The third sense of 'fides' is a pledged security under an agreement, which must be kept even toward an enemy (Decretum C.23 q.1).
claims: 'Fides' can mean a pledged agreement binding even toward enemies.

jhbl1q2-d1e5061.summary: The fourth sense of 'fides' is conscience, as in the canonistic titles on witnesses and on prescription (good faith).
claims: 'Fides' can mean conscience or good faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e5067.summary: The fifth sense of 'fides' is credulity, by which we believe what we have not seen, as in Gregory's saying that faith has no merit where reason provides proof.
claims: 'Fides' can mean belief in what is not seen.

jhbl1q2-d1e5074.summary: The sixth sense of 'fides' is the collection of the articles of faith. The Pauline definition (Hebrews 11, 'substance of things hoped for, argument of things not seen') is then given, which Hostiensis judges insufficient for two reasons; the first is that it also fits hope (with a reference to Lombard, Sent. III d.24).
claims: 'Fides' can mean the body of articles.
The definition in Hebrews 11 is insufficient because it also applies to hope.

jhbl1q2-d1e5107.summary: Hostiensis's second objection is that the Hebrews definition speaks only of future things, so it is a description, not a definition (Lombard, III d.26). The alternative definition, 'faith is a voluntary certitude about absent things, below science and above opinion', is judged false as to certitude: faith's adhesive certitude is no less than that of evident science, though faith ranks below science in evidence. William of Auxerre and Giles of Rome are cited.
claims: Faith is not less certain than science in firmness of adhesion.
Faith is below science only in evidence, not in certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e5138.summary: Defines the sixth term, 'adherence of faith', following Hugolino: a certitude of judgment, greater than any the wayfarer has, by which one adheres to something not evidently known but believed to be revealed by the First Truth. Hugh of St Victor's definitions of faith as certitude about absent things above opinion and below science are cited in support, the 'below science' to be read as regarding evidence. This ends the second article.
claims: Adherence of faith is a certitude greater than any other a wayfarer has, resting on revelation, not evidence.
Faith is below science in evidence but not in certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e5190.summary: Opens the third article with the first conclusion: the law of the Christian sect is binding on every rational creature and condemns every erroneous sect.
claims: The Christian law binds every rational creature.
The Christian law condemns every erroneous sect.

jhbl1q2-d1e5193.summary: Proves the first part: every rational creature is bound to love God and neighbor, and on these two commandments the whole law depends (Matthew 22), so every rational creature is bound to the Christian law.
claims: Every rational creature is obliged to love God and neighbor.
The Christian law is summed up in the two love commandments.

jhbl1q2-d1e5211.summary: Second proof: every rational nature is bound by the eternal and unchangeable law (Cicero, De legibus I, as worked out in an earlier principium), and the Christian law is transcribed from it immediately, or at least through natural law.
claims: Every rational nature is bound by eternal law.
Christian law derives from eternal law directly or through natural law.

jhbl1q2-d1e5231.summary: Third proof, from the last chapters of Mark and Matthew (the great commission to teach all nations).
claims: Christ's commission makes the law binding universally.

jhbl1q2-d1e5245.summary: Proves the second part (the Christian law condemns every erroneous sect) from Augustine's De doctrina christiana II: whatever a person learns outside Scripture is condemned there if harmful and found there if useful.
claims: Whatever is harmful is condemned in Scripture, and whatever is useful is found there.

jhbl1q2-d1e5268.summary: First corollary: God's just precept binds even damned natures to willing well justly, since as rational natures they are bound to love God and neighbor, which is impossible without just good willing.
claims: The damned remain bound by God's precept to will well.

jhbl1q2-d1e5271.summary: Second corollary: a damned angel is obliged to lay aside its deformed will even though this is impossible for it, both because otherwise it would not be obstinate and because the love of God it owes requires it.
claims: A damned angel is obliged to give up its evil will even though it cannot.

jhbl1q2-d1e5274.summary: Third corollary: every doctrine asserting the opposite or contrary of the Christian law is error, not science, since the law is true (otherwise it would not oblige) and truth cannot contradict truth. Hence the truth of the Christian sect is not only true but sincere.
claims: Any teaching contrary to the Christian law is error.
Truth does not contradict truth.
The truth of the Christian sect is 'sincere' (unmixed with falsity).

jhbl1q2-d1e5283.summary: Second principal conclusion: under the present order (lege stante) no wayfarer knows any sincere truth perfectly, absolutely and intuitively; yet whatever is known through theological science is known more perfectly than through the evidence of any other created science available to the wayfarer.
claims: Under the present order no wayfarer has perfect intuitive knowledge of any sincere truth.
Whatever theology knows, it knows more perfectly than any other created science of the wayfarer.

jhbl1q2-d1e5286.summary: Proves the first part: no wayfarer properly, perfectly and intuitively knows the specific or individual differences of things, and such knowledge is what knowing a thing perfectly and intuitively requires.
claims: Wayfarers do not know the specific or individual differences of things intuitively.

jhbl1q2-d1e5293.summary: Second proof: under the present order the wayfarer's intellect cannot evidently and infallibly intuit the presence or nature of any substance, as the sacrament of the altar shows (the substance of bread is absent though the appearances remain).
claims: The wayfarer cannot infallibly intuit the presence of any substance.
The Eucharist shows that appearances do not guarantee the presence of substance.

jhbl1q2-d1e5299.summary: Third proof: no created object suffices to represent itself as an object; another light is needed. The light of the agent intellect is insufficient for perfect, proper, intuitive representation, because it originates from fallible phantasms.
claims: No created object suffices for its own objective representation.
The light of the agent intellect, arising from phantasms, cannot give perfect intuitive representation.

jhbl1q2-d1e5312.summary: Proves the second part: whatever theology knows, actually or habitually, it knows as represented ideally, eternally and perfectly in the triune God and as freely producible or produced in time. No other science knows its objects this way, so theological knowledge is more perfect.
claims: Theology knows things as ideally represented in the triune God and as freely produced by him.
No other science knows its objects in this way.

jhbl1q2-d1e5318.summary: Grounds the first part of the conclusion in Hermann of Schildesche (Postilla on the Song of Songs) and in Hugolino's fivefold division of cognitions: (1) the infinite substantial intuition that is God; (2) the clear exemplar beatific vision; (3) the enigmatic, inevident adherence of faith, an infallible revelation; (4) a pure, clear intellectual intuition of a thing in its own kind, unimpeded by body or phantasm; (5) natural intuitive cognition caused through phantasms and sense. The conclusion denies the wayfarer the fourth kind.
claims: There are five grades of cognition, from God's self-intuition down to phantasm-based natural intuition.
The wayfarer lacks pure intellectual intuition unimpeded by phantasms.

jhbl1q2-d1e5345.summary: First corollary, in Henry of Ghent's formulation: under the present order no mere wayfarer can have infallible, sincere certitude of evidence about any created thing without the eternal exemplar, since such certitude would be perfect intellectual intuition, which the conclusion excludes.
claims: Infallible, sincere certitude about creatures requires the eternal exemplar.

jhbl1q2-d1e5357.summary: Second corollary: not every certitude that excludes all error is sincere certitude or perfectly intuitive evident knowledge, since the former is possible without the eternal exemplar and the latter is not. On this basis Hiltalingen defends Henry of Ghent against misreadings: Henry neither denied all certain knowledge of creatures nor denied that we can have any knowledge of things in their eternal exemplar.
claims: Error-free certitude is distinct from sincere, perfectly intuitive certitude.
Henry of Ghent did not deny all certain knowledge of creatures.
Henry did not deny all knowledge of things in their eternal exemplar in this life.

jhbl1q2-d1e5387.summary: Third corollary, taken from Giles of Rome: although the sincere truth of theological science is maximally abstract and special, since its primary object is maximally simple and one, it treats everything most perfectly, following from the conclusion's second part.
claims: Theology's primary object is maximally simple and one.
Theology nevertheless treats all things most perfectly.

jhbl1q2-d1e5413.summary: Third principal conclusion: Christian faith is a firm certitude that falls short of theology as knowledge or evidence, yet is first required for it.
claims: Faith is a firm certitude.
Faith is less than theology as knowledge or evidence.
Faith is required first, as the precondition of theology.

jhbl1q2-d1e5423.summary: The first part, that faith is a firm certitude, follows from the definitions of the fifth and sixth terms in the second article.

jhbl1q2-d1e5430.summary: Proves the second part: faith is some kind of knowledge (Augustine: faith has its own eyes; to believe is to think with assent; Hugh; Lombard: knowledge begins from faith), but less than theology, since according to Augustine (De Trinitate XIV) many of the faithful are strong in faith without being strong in this science.
claims: Faith is a kind of cognition.
Many have strong faith without theological science, so theology exceeds faith as knowledge.

jhbl1q2-d1e5484.summary: Proves the third part, that faith is first required, from Pseudo-Dionysius (De divinis nominibus 2): one who resists the divine oracles is far from our wisdom.
claims: Rejecting the divine words cuts one off from theological wisdom.

jhbl1q2-d1e5509.summary: Further proof from Anselm (Cur Deus homo I.1): believers seek reasons not to reach faith through reason but to delight in understanding and contemplating what they already believe.
claims: Rational inquiry in theology presupposes faith and aims at understanding it.

jhbl1q2-d1e5536.summary: Further proof from Anselm: right order requires that we first believe the depths of the Christian faith before presuming to discuss them by reason.
claims: Belief must precede rational discussion of the faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e5556.summary: Further proof from Augustine (De vera innocentia): faith opens the way to understanding and unbelief closes it. The part is therefore true, and Gregory of Rimini proves it at length.
claims: Faith opens and unbelief closes access to understanding.

jhbl1q2-d1e5578.summary: First corollary: the foundation of Christian faith has as much adhesive certitude as the conclusion of the most powerful demonstration. Faith is so firm that it is simply impossible for it to be false, falsity cannot fall under it, and infused faith tends toward its supernatural object as properly as a natural habit tends toward its natural object.
claims: Faith has adhesive certitude equal to that of demonstrative conclusions.
Nothing false can fall under faith.
Infused faith is ordered to its supernatural object as a natural habit to its object.

jhbl1q2-d1e5581.summary: Second corollary: Christian faith is not as great in knowledge or cognition as it is in firmness or certitude, since it has less cognition than theology or a demonstrative conclusion but equal certitude. Against Gregory of Rimini and Gottschalk, theology is therefore not merely acquired faith but a further knowledge beyond faith in cognition and evidence.
claims: Faith's certitude exceeds its cognitive evidence.
Theology is not merely acquired faith but adds cognition and evidence beyond faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e5593.summary: Third corollary, against Brinkel: the faith of the Christian sect suffices per se and immediately to inform the intellect of the sincere truth, without requiring additional evidence extrinsic to faith. Otherwise assent to some article would depend on extrinsic evidence not in the believer's power, and no one could be damned for unbelief, contrary to Augustine (De utilitate credendi), Henry of Ghent, and Hugolino's report of Parisian masters such as Holcot.
claims: Faith suffices by itself to inform the intellect about the truth of the faith.
If assent required extrinsic evidence, unbelief would not be culpable.

jhbl1q2-d1e5647.summary: Fourth principal conclusion: under the present order a wayfarer can know the sincere truth of Christianity assertively through the foundation of faith or a supernatural ray; yet someone can also have the habit and act of faith while believing no article of the Catholic faith.
claims: The truth of the faith can be known assertively through faith or supernatural light.
One can have the habit and act of faith without believing any article.

jhbl1q2-d1e5650.summary: The first part follows from the third conclusion and from Scripture: 1 Corinthians 3 (no one can lay another foundation), Galatians 5 (only faith avails in Christ), and Romans 1 / Habakkuk 2 ('the just shall live by faith').
claims: Faith is the foundation through which the truth of Christianity is known.

jhbl1q2-d1e5691.summary: Proves the second part (illumination or faith is required) from Augustine: he cannot lead anyone into understanding such a secret unless God aids the mind. Henry of Ghent cites this at length, and Augustine's De libero arbitrio is added.
claims: Understanding the divine mysteries requires God's help.

jhbl1q2-d1e5733.summary: Continues with Augustine (De libero arbitrio): people who wish to understand rather than believe must still take refuge in the authority of the law, and no one is fit to find God unless he first believes.
claims: No one is fit to find God without first believing.

jhbl1q2-d1e5740.summary: Proves the last part, against Gregory of Rimini and Gottschalk, by divine power: the act of faith is no more identical with its actuating than an accident is with its inhering. Since God can make an accident without its inhering, he can make the act of faith without its believing anything, so one can have faith's habit and act without believing any article.
claims: The act of faith is really distinct from its actual believing, as an accident is from its inherence.
By divine power the act of faith can exist without actually believing any article.

jhbl1q2-d1e5759.summary: First corollary: many are saved without believing any sect at all, such as baptized children dying before adulthood and baptized persons naturally lacking the use of reason.
claims: Baptized infants and baptized people without the use of reason are saved without explicit belief.

jhbl1q2-d1e5764.summary: Second corollary: in some sect more people are saved than would be damned if they believed, as with baptized Greek children who die before the age of discretion.
claims: Baptized children of the Greek church dying before discretion are saved.

jhbl1q2-d1e5767.summary: Third corollary: not everyone who fails to believe as the Roman Church believes and justly commands errs in believing, since one may licitly believe nothing for a time. Thus Christ's 'he who does not believe will be condemned' (Mark 16) and the Athanasian Creed should be read of the faith that one is able to have, which answers possible objections.
claims: One may licitly believe nothing for a time without erring.
The condemnations of unbelief apply to those capable of believing.

jhbl1q2-d1e5795.summary: Fifth principal conclusion: under the present order the sincere truth of Christianity can be adequately had through sensible signs and miracles, through what is said and believed, and through infused lights, and not otherwise.
claims: The truth of Christianity is had only through signs and miracles, testimony and belief, and infused light.

jhbl1q2-d1e5804.summary: Proves the first part, against Brinkel: a true moral philosopher who saw Christ and his disciples living morally well and performing wonders that no natural power can effect would be compelled to acknowledge a supernatural power, as Christ argued in John 10 ('believe the works').
claims: Wonders beyond natural power compel acknowledgment of supernatural power.
A rational observer of Christ's works must confess their supernatural source.

jhbl1q2-d1e5828.summary: Adds texts from John 3, 4, 9, 15 and Matthew 27, and the analogy of an astronomer who sees an eclipse at full moon or the sun standing still at a man's command and must likewise confess a supernatural cause. He cites FitzRalph's Summa de quaestionibus Armenorum and Bradwardine (De causa Dei I.1) for the probative force of miracles, and defers the other parts to the third and fourth conclusions and to Book III d.1 (whether Christ's divine sonship can be proved from the Old Testament).
claims: Astronomically impossible events, such as an eclipse at full moon, compel acknowledgment of a supernatural cause.
Sensible miracles suffice to prove the Christian faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e5888.summary: Also defers to the beginning of Book IV, where it will be asked whether the Christian law abrogates the old legal precepts, and so stops here.

jhbl1q2-d1e5893.summary: First corollary: one should rely more on Catholic Scripture than on the dictate of reason or natural evidence (Matthew 5, 'not one iota shall pass from the law'; Romans 1; Hugolino's commentary on Dionysius's Celestial Hierarchy).
claims: Scripture is to be relied on more than reason or natural evidence.

jhbl1q2-d1e5926.summary: Second corollary: everything believed in the Christian faith can be shown or revealed to a wayfarer remaining within the limits of this life, since its sacred content cannot lead him beyond those limits, as Thomas of Strasbourg argues.
claims: Everything believed can be revealed to a wayfarer within the bounds of this life.

jhbl1q2-d1e5935.summary: Third corollary: under the common law (the ordinary order) no wayfarer can assertively know the sincere truth of Christianity without God's illumination and the foundation of Catholic faith, since such knowledge comes only from signs, testimony, or infused lights. What God could do by absolute power is outside the question.
claims: Under the ordinary order the truth of Christianity cannot be known without illumination and faith.
The question concerns God's ordained, not absolute, power.

jhbl1q2-d1e5945.summary: Draws the result of the third article: the question, as formulated, is true.
claims: The question is answered affirmatively.

jhbl1q2-d1e5955.summary: Opens the fourth article, which raises objections against what has been said, beginning with objections to the definitions of terms given in the second article.

jhbl1q2-d1e5960.summary: Objects to the second sense of 'truth': the complexly signifiable is nothing but the things signified by the terms of the proposition, which are not distinct from what is signified incomplexly, so the distinction collapses.
claims: The complexe significabile reduces to the things signified by the terms.

jhbl1q2-d1e5963.summary: Objects to the third sense: if a proposition is properly a truth, then since a proposition can be false, a truth could be false, which is absurd.
claims: Calling propositions truths would imply that a truth can be false.

jhbl1q2-d1e5975.summary: Objects to the first sense: every thing is complexly signifiable and every complexly signifiable is incomplexly signifiable, so distinguishing the first sense seems pointless.
claims: Complex and incomplex signifiables are coextensive.

jhbl1q2-d1e5990.summary: Objects to the definition of the Christian sect: Christ is a member of the Church, so he cannot be its principal shepherd or head without being head of himself.
claims: If Christ is a member of the Church he cannot be its head.
concepts: Christ as head of the Church

jhbl1q2-d1e5993.summary: A second objection to the same definition: it would follow that only those in grace belong to the Christian sect, since only they are under the precepts of God and Christ, and this is false.
claims: The definition wrongly restricts the Church to those in grace.

jhbl1q2-d1e5996.summary: A third objection: it would follow that no excommunicated person belongs to the Christian sect, since such a person is not obediently united with the others, and this is false.
claims: The definition wrongly excludes the excommunicated from the Church.

jhbl1q2-d1e6001.summary: Objects to the definition of reason: it would make syllogistic form a 'reason', since syllogistic form makes the truth of an unknown proposition known. The objector also asks what such a reason would be, whether act, habit, species, or substitute for a species, and argues that it fits none of these and so is nothing.
claims: The definition counts syllogistic form as reason.
Reason so defined fits no ontological category of mental items.

jhbl1q2-d1e6008.summary: A further objection: on the definition, joy, pain and the other passions would be reasons, since they immediately make some otherwise unknown proposition known to the intellect.
claims: The definition would wrongly include the passions as reasons.

jhbl1q2-d1e6017.summary: Objects to the first sense of illumination: illumination is a mental art of the soul, and Augustine says that art is nothing but the soul; since God is not the soul, illumination cannot be God.
claims: Illumination is an art of the soul, and art is the soul itself.
Therefore illumination is not God.

jhbl1q2-d1e6034.summary: Objects to the second sense of illumination (as motion): such a motion would be the motion either of a power or of a thing existing in potency, and it is neither.
claims: Illumination cannot be a motion of a power or of something in potency.

jhbl1q2-d1e6037.summary: Objects to the third sense (illumination as act): the act would proceed either from the power alone actively, which cannot be said, or from the power and the object together, which would let a bodily object act on spirit, contrary to Augustine, De musica VI. Richard and John of Marchia are cited, the latter also treating how art is the soul itself.
claims: A bodily object cannot act on spirit (Augustine).
The illuminated act cannot be accounted for by power alone or power plus object.

jhbl1q2-d1e6061.summary: Objects to the definition of faith that there is no supernatural habit. If there were, its possessor could know that he has it and so know the article it concerns to be true; and since the habit relates equally to every article, knowing one would mean knowing all, which is implausible.
claims: Whoever knows he has faith in an article knows that article to be true.
The habit of faith relates equally to every article.
concepts: unity of the habit of faith

jhbl1q2-d1e6064.summary: A second objection to the definition of faith: there is no supernatural truth, since the soul can naturally know the first principle, in which every truth is virtually contained, and so can naturally know every truth.
claims: Every truth is virtually contained in the first principle.
Knowing the first principle naturally implies being able to know all truth naturally.

jhbl1q2-d1e6067.summary: Further objection: the soul suffers no violence in perceiving divine truths, so such perception is not supernatural to it.
claims: What is perceived without violence to the soul is natural to it.

jhbl1q2-d1e6080.summary: Further objection: man is now of the same species as in the state of innocence, when no truth would have been supernatural to him, so none is supernatural now.
claims: In the state of innocence no truth was supernatural to man.

jhbl1q2-d1e6085.summary: A third objection to the definition of faith: it conflicts with Hebrews 11. Everything cognitively perceived is apparent, whereas faith according to the Apostle concerns things not apparent, so faith cannot be a habit for cognitively perceiving.
claims: Whatever is cognitively perceived is apparent.
Faith concerns what is not apparent.

jhbl1q2-d1e6102.summary: Objects to the definition of the adherence of faith: following Michael of Massa (as reported by Alphonsus and Thomas of Strasbourg), the adherence of faith includes fear of the opposite, so it is not the highest certitude.
claims: Adherence of faith includes formido oppositi.

jhbl1q2-d1e6119.summary: Second objection: the adherence of faith is not the greatest certitude, since a first principle is more certain; no one can contradict a principle, but very many contradict the faith.
claims: First principles are more certain than faith because no one can deny them.

jhbl1q2-d1e6122.summary: Third objection: faith would both exceed and be exceeded by the same thing, since it is said to be the highest certitude and yet a weaker cognition.
claims: Faith cannot be both highest in certitude and inferior in cognition.

jhbl1q2-d1e6132.summary: Objects to the first part of the first conclusion: the Christian law has not been given to many people, so it does not bind them (John 15, 'if I had not come they would have no sin'). That it has not reached all is shown from Matthew 24: the gospel will be preached to all nations before the end, and the end has not yet come.
claims: A law not promulgated does not bind.
The gospel has not yet been preached to all nations.

jhbl1q2-d1e6158.summary: Second objection: every wayfarer who fails to conform to the law would then sin, which is false of unbaptized infants, who have only original sin.
claims: Unbaptized infants do not conform to the law yet commit no actual sin.

jhbl1q2-d1e6163.summary: Further instance: the invincibly ignorant, whose ignorance excuses from sin.
claims: Invincible ignorance excuses from sin.

jhbl1q2-d1e6166.summary: Further objection: an unbeliever deviates from the law equally throughout his life, so he would sin continuously and thus infinitely many times, which is false.
claims: Continuous non-conformity would entail infinitely many sins.

jhbl1q2-d1e6172.summary: Objects to the second part of the first conclusion: the rule of the Christian law is not adequately commensurate with the divine law, so one can err from divine law in ways the Christian rule cannot detect or correct; hence it does not condemn every erroneous sect.
claims: The Christian law is not adequately commensurate with divine law.
Therefore it cannot reprove every error.

jhbl1q2-d1e6194.summary: Objects to the first two corollaries (the damned remain obliged): it would follow that the damned continually become worse. But the blessed do not continually become better, and the damned are as fixed in obstinacy as the blessed are in confirmation.
claims: The damned do not continually grow worse.
Confirmation of the blessed parallels obstinacy of the damned.

jhbl1q2-d1e6197.summary: Second objection: it would follow that the damned continually sin anew and demerit, which is false since they are outside the state of the way, where merit and demerit occur.
claims: The damned are beyond the state of meriting and demeriting.

jhbl1q2-d1e6205.summary: Objects to the third corollary (every doctrine contrary to the Christian law is error): philosophy would then be error rather than science, since it holds things contrary to the faith, such as the eternity of the world and the perpetuity of celestial motion.
claims: Philosophy teaches doctrines contrary to faith, such as the eternity of the world.

jhbl1q2-d1e6210.summary: Objects to the second principal conclusion with Augustine (De videndo Deo, to Paulina): I see my own will clearly within, as I see bodily light by sense, so the wayfarer does have clear intuitive knowledge of something.
claims: We clearly intuit our own will.

jhbl1q2-d1e6230.summary: Further from Augustine (De Trinitate XIII.2): each person's own will is plainly evident to him, so the first part of the conclusion is false.
claims: One's own will is evident to oneself.

jhbl1q2-d1e6242.summary: Objects to the second part: in other sciences a conclusion reduced to first principles, such as the common conceptions ('every whole is greater than its part'), is known with a certitude than which none is more perfect, so theology cannot know more perfectly. Gregory of Rimini and Hugolino could be cited.
claims: Knowledge reduced to self-evident principles has unsurpassable certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e6259.summary: Objects to the first corollary of the second conclusion: Aristotle had many certitudes, defining many things, without the eternal exemplar, which he rejected against Plato.
claims: Aristotle had certain knowledge while rejecting eternal exemplars.

jhbl1q2-d1e6276.summary: Objects to the second corollary with Augustine: truth never suffers falsity and is corrupted only by mixture with falsity (83 Questions; De mendacio), so any certitude excluding all error is sincere.
claims: Truth is impaired only by admixture of falsity.

jhbl1q2-d1e6291.summary: Objects to the third corollary: a science's commonness follows from the commonness of its subject (Giles), and theology's subject is common, since according to Lombard it treats things and signs, so theology is common rather than maximally special.
claims: The generality of a science follows from the generality of its subject.
Theology's subject (res et signa) is common.

jhbl1q2-d1e6314.summary: Objects to the third conclusion with a trilemma based on Durandus (via Thomas of Strasbourg): theology would be superior to faith either as creditive (but then it is Scripture, no more evident than faith), as defensive (but it cannot defend the faith by a reason superior to faith), or as elicitive (but there is no evidence in it that is not or cannot be in faith).
claims: Theology is not superior to faith as creditive, defensive, or elicitive.

jhbl1q2-d1e6338.summary: Second objection: faith and theology are either the same habit (against the conclusion) or different. If different, suppose both are uniformly diminished: either they cease together, and so are equal, or faith ceases first, and theology then remains without faith, so faith is not necessarily prior.
claims: If faith and theology are distinct habits, theology could survive the loss of faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e6341.summary: Third objection: the evidence of each truth equals its certitude, and its knowledge equals its evidence, so knowledge equals certitude, against the claim that faith's certitude exceeds its knowledge; every degree of certitude is a degree of evidence.
claims: Certitude, evidence, and knowledge are proportionate for every truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e6344.summary: Supports the major premise: every proposition is as evident to God as it is certain, so the same holds of every truth.
claims: For God, evidence and certitude coincide.

jhbl1q2-d1e6350.summary: Objects to the first corollary (faith as certain as demonstration): things are not equally certain if one can freely assent or dissent to the first but cannot dissent from the second. As Augustine says, one cannot believe unless willing, so a believer can freely not believe, but no one can dissent from the conclusion of a strict demonstration.
claims: Belief is free; assent to demonstration is necessary.
What can be freely withheld is less certain.

jhbl1q2-d1e6362.summary: Objects to the second corollary: if faith is infinite certitude but only finite knowledge, the same thing would be finite and infinite.
claims: Faith cannot be both infinite in certitude and finite in knowledge.

jhbl1q2-d1e6367.summary: Turns to the third corollary (faith alone causes assent). Holcot's arguments are skipped since Hugolino reports and answers them, and Brinkel's are presented. First: the intellect assents to a proposition that is not self-evident only through some discursive application, so faith does not immediately cause assent.
claims: Assent to non-self-evident propositions requires discursive mediation.

jhbl1q2-d1e6388.summary: Brinkel's second argument: nothing immediately causes assent to an article if an act of dissent toward that same article can coexist with it. Yet simple believers of great faith hold erroneous beliefs about the Incarnation (for example that Christ did not exist before the Virgin bore him), so faith coexists with dissent.
claims: Faith can coexist with dissent from an article in simple believers.
What coexists with dissent does not per se cause assent.

jhbl1q2-d1e6392.summary: Brinkel's third argument: if the habit of faith were infused into someone, that person would not thereby assent to any article, so faith does not per se and immediately cause assent, since otherwise its effect would follow upon it.
claims: Infused faith alone does not yield assent to any article.

jhbl1q2-d1e6405.summary: Objects to the fourth conclusion with arguments of Francis of Marchia (reported by Gregory of Rimini) and of 'Olsensus': the knowledge of Christianity is self-evident or deduced from self-evident principles, since no one is bound to believe indubitably what is not so, and everyone is bound to believe its truth indubitably; therefore faith is not needed to apprehend it.
claims: No one is bound to believe indubitably what is neither self-evident nor deduced from what is.
Everyone is bound to believe Christianity indubitably.

jhbl1q2-d1e6421.summary: Second Marchian argument: a per se false proposition, such as 'God does not exist', is indubitably false to everyone, so the per se true is equally indubitably true; the truths of Christianity are of this kind.
claims: 'God does not exist' is per se false.
The truths of Christianity are per se true.

jhbl1q2-d1e6424.summary: Third argument: the truths of the faith cannot form an infinite series, so there must be some first believed principle(s). These are believed either because of another believed truth (excluded), because of something self-evident, or for their own sake, and in either of the last cases they are self-evident. William of Auxerre treats this.
claims: There is no infinite regress among the truths of faith.
First principles of faith must be believed for their own sake and so be self-evident.

jhbl1q2-d1e6436.summary: Objects to the first corollary of the fourth conclusion (some are saved without believing any sect): the gospel texts, especially the final chapters, and the Athanasian Creed seem to oppose it.
claims: Scripture and the Athanasian Creed require faith for salvation.

jhbl1q2-d1e6448.summary: Objects to the second corollary: a child of another sect reaching the age of discretion seems licitly able, in his first act, to believe his sect true and not be damned if he dies immediately, since the ignorance that excused him before still excuses him.
claims: Invincible ignorance excuses one who first comes to the use of reason in another sect.

jhbl1q2-d1e6466.summary: Objects to the third corollary: the head must rule the members, and the Roman Church is head of all (Christ calls Peter 'Cephas', i.e. head), so everyone is bound to believe as it believes.
claims: The Roman Church is head of all and all must believe as it believes.

jhbl1q2-d1e6485.summary: Objects to the fifth conclusion: if its first part were true, sensible signs and miracles would by themselves and immediately suffice to make the Christian sect evidently probable.

jhbl1q2-d1e6488.summary: Gives Brinkel's argument against this: since the sensitive power can judge erroneously through some sensation, it can judge erroneously through any. Because Brinkel's other arguments all rest on the fallibility of sense about the objects of faith, only this one is given, and its answer will cover the rest.
claims: The senses are fallible in their judgments.
Fallible sense cannot by itself prove the faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e6496.summary: Objects to the second part (truth through testimony): according to Augustine, as cited by William of Auxerre, some things are believed only after being understood, so they cannot be had merely from testimony.
claims: Some things must be understood before they are believed.

jhbl1q2-d1e6507.summary: Objects to the third part (truth through infused lights) on the astrological principle of Albumasar and other astronomers, reported by Brinkel: religions arise from conjunctions of the superior planets, not from signs, testimony or infused lights.
claims: Religions originate from planetary conjunctions (Albumasar).

jhbl1q2-d1e6525.summary: Objects to the first corollary of the fifth conclusion (Scripture over reason): we rely on Scripture because of Christ's words, yet it is sometimes right to rely on reason over Christ's words, as when Peter licitly disbelieved Christ's prediction that he would deny him three times.
claims: Peter licitly disbelieved Christ's prediction of the denial.

jhbl1q2-d1e6535.summary: Objects to the second corollary with Giles of Rome (Quodlibet V q.6): no wayfarer can be necessitated to love God, yet one who sees God clearly is so necessitated, so no wayfarer can see God clearly; Anselm's De libertate arbitrii supports the first premise. Thomas of Strasbourg treats this at length, and this ends the fourth article.
claims: Clear vision of God necessitates love of God.
A wayfarer cannot be necessitated to love God.
So no wayfarer sees God clearly.

jhbl1q2-d1e6570.summary: Opens the fifth and final article, which answers the objections in the order in which they were raised.

jhbl1q2-d1e6575.summary: Replies to the first objection against the senses of 'truth': the distinction followed the common usage of many authors and claimed only that the word is used in these ways by the doctors, whether rightly or wrongly.
claims: The threefold distinction of 'truth' records usage, not a metaphysical commitment.

jhbl1q2-d1e6578.summary: Second, even if the complexly signifiable is the incomplex thing itself and vice versa, it is connoted differently when signified complexly than when signified incomplexly, and this suffices for the distinction.
claims: The same thing signified complexly and incomplexly differs in connotation, which grounds the distinction.

jhbl1q2-d1e6582.summary: Third, 'true' and 'truth' are predicable of many things that are not incomplexly signifiable statements, and that is why the second member of the distinction was posited.

jhbl1q2-d1e6592.summary: Replies to the objection that a truth could be false: taking the terms concretely, he grants the consequent, since it then means only that a true proposition can be false, which is true.
claims: A true proposition can become false, so in the concrete sense a 'truth' can be false.

jhbl1q2-d1e6597.summary: Replies to the objection that every thing is complexly and incomplexly signifiable by distinguishing: if 'incomplexly signifiable' means by a non-transcendental term signifying a determinate substance or nature, the consequence holds but the antecedent is false; if it means by any term including a transcendental, the antecedent holds but the consequence fails.
claims: Not everything is incomplexly signifiable by a determinate (non-transcendental) term.

jhbl1q2-d1e6605.summary: Answers the objection that Christ cannot be head of the Church he belongs to by distinguishing three senses of 'Church': (1) the universal congregation of the faithful; (2) the mystical body of Christ, head and members united; (3) the prelates and pastors (Matthew 18, 'tell it to the Church'). Christ is a member of the Church in the second sense while being principal pastor in the first or third, as William of Auxerre explains.
claims: 'Church' has three senses: congregation of the faithful, mystical body, and hierarchy of prelates.
Christ can be a member of the mystical body and also head and shepherd of the Church.

jhbl1q2-d1e6641.summary: As further help, gives Marsilius of Padua's distinction of the senses of 'ecclesia' (Defensor pacis II): in Greek usage, an assembly of people under one government (Aristotle, Politics II); among Latins, a building where God is worshipped (1 Corinthians 11); and the priests, bishops and ministers.
claims: 'Ecclesia' can mean a civic assembly, a church building, or the clergy.

jhbl1q2-d1e6674.summary: Continues Marsilius: 'Church' can also mean the ministers of the Roman Church, pope and cardinals, and, most properly and originally in apostolic usage, the whole body of faithful who believe in and invoke Christ's name, including any part of it (1 Corinthians 1, Acts 20, Ephesians 5). Hugh of St Victor's definition of the Church as the body of Christ, vivified by one Spirit and united in one faith, the 'universitas Christianorum', resolves the first objection.
claims: The primary and apostolic sense of 'Church' is the totality of believers.
'Church' applies both to the whole body of believers and to its parts.

jhbl1q2-d1e6707.summary: Answers the second and third objections (the definition excludes sinners and the excommunicated): the precepts of the Christian sect are twofold, those distinguishing believer from unbeliever and those distinguishing good from bad believers. The definition concerns the first, while the objections assume the second.
claims: Membership in the Church depends on precepts distinguishing believer from unbeliever, not good from bad believer.

jhbl1q2-d1e6716.summary: Answers the first objection to the definition of reason by denying that syllogistic form follows as a 'reason' and rejecting the proof.
claims: Syllogistic form is not ratio in the defined sense.

jhbl1q2-d1e6724.summary: Explains why: syllogistic form alone does not suffice, and immediacy is twofold, of inference and of adherence; the definition concerns immediacy of adherence. A formally valid consequence is not thereby recognized as valid by every intellect, just as a sophistical argument can seem demonstrative and a demonstrative one can seem sophistical.
claims: Immediacy of inference differs from immediacy of adherence.
Formal validity does not guarantee recognition of validity.

jhbl1q2-d1e6730.summary: Answers the question about the ontological status of reason: the division offered is insufficient, since reason can be called a natural power, which the Philosopher places in the second species of quality (Categories).
claims: Reason can be classified as a natural power, a quality of the second species.

jhbl1q2-d1e6739.summary: Answers the objection about the passions by denying the consequence. He reports Brinkel's reply, that passions do not lead the intellect abstractively, but judges it inadequate on his own definition, which also includes deduction. His own answer is that passions do not lead intellectually to knowledge but rather through sensory experience, which the definition does not cover.
claims: Passions make things known by sensory experience, not intellectually, so they are not reasons.

jhbl1q2-d1e6759.summary: Begins the reply to Augustine's 'art is nothing but the soul' by distinguishing senses of 'art'. First, art is the habitude for artfully changing something, the first act of any art.
claims: 'Ars' can denote a habitude or first act for artful change.

jhbl1q2-d1e6770.summary: Second, art is the actual artful change, which is either uncreated (art essentially and substantively, i.e. God) or created (art only denominatively, when something is perceived through it). The soul's art, taken as aptitude or first act, is nothing but the soul, as Augustine says; taken as that which vitally changes the soul, it is not the soul, and in this sense God can be the soul's art. So the objection's conversion fails, as John of Marchia also explains.
claims: Uncreated art is art essentially; created art is art only denominatively.
As aptitude, the soul's art is the soul; as what vitally moves the soul, it can be God.

jhbl1q2-d1e6789.summary: Answers whether the motion of illumination belongs to a power or to a thing in potency: John of Marchia would say a power, while James of Viterbo (Quodlibet I q.12) would say it is a motion proceeding from the soul through natural aptitudes (idoneitates) existing in it.
claims: The motion of illumination belongs to a power (Marchia) or comes from the soul through natural aptitudes (James of Viterbo).

jhbl1q2-d1e6804.summary: Raises a doubt about James's aptitudes: if they are the same as the soul, how does the same thing move itself, and if not, the view seems untenable. Without settling it, he distinguishes a perceptible's entitative presence to a perceptive power from its objective presence, and says the motion of illumination is simply what makes an object objectively or vitally present.
claims: Presence of a perceptible to a power is either entitative or objective.
The motion of illumination makes an object objectively present.

jhbl1q2-d1e6811.summary: Adds that this objective presence may come about either by moving the perceptive power or by recalling the perceptible, and defers further treatment to another place.

jhbl1q2-d1e6814.summary: Answers the third objection (the source of the illuminated act): on Hugolino's view the act proceeds from both the power and the object, while on Marchia's and Richard's view it proceeds only from the intelligible species, not the object. Either way the act is caused through such a motion, which is enough for his definition.
claims: The illuminated act is caused through the cognitive motion, whatever its further source.

jhbl1q2-d1e6842.summary: Begins the reply to 'there is no supernatural habit' by explaining what a supernatural habit properly is. Scotus's first mode: a receptive power compared to the act it receives is never supernatural, but compared to the agent from which it receives, it is natural when that agent naturally impresses the form and supernatural when it does not, as with the possible and agent intellect.
claims: Supernaturality is a matter of the receptive power's relation to the agent, not to the form received.

jhbl1q2-d1e6873.summary: Scotus's second mode: information by an agent that supplies the place of a supernatural object, namely the triune God in his own nature, is supernatural. Brinkel argues against the first mode: had man not sinned he would have received this form naturally, since it was a means to his natural ultimate end; man is the same species now, so it is natural now, and the intellect naturally desires the means to its end as it desires the end.
claims: A habit supplying the place of the triune God as object is supernatural (Scotus).
Brinkel: what would have been natural in innocence is natural now.

jhbl1q2-d1e6893.summary: Brinkel's third argument is that the intellect can receive action naturally from the agent 'being in general', and so from God, since being is univocal. Brinkel then proposes his own account: forms relate to a power as violent, neutral, or natural, and a form is supernatural when it cannot be acquired from the coordination of secondary causes together with God's general concurrence. Hiltalingen notes that Brinkel's 'precisely from the coordination' seems to exclude all divine influence.
claims: A supernatural form cannot be acquired through secondary causes with God's general concurrence (Brinkel).
Brinkel's formulation risks excluding divine influence.

jhbl1q2-d1e6920.summary: Leaves to the studious reader whether Brinkel's arguments against Scotus succeed, suggesting they could easily be answered.
claims: Brinkel's arguments against Scotus are easily answerable.

jhbl1q2-d1e6929.summary: Introduces another way of answering, based on Thomas of Strasbourg (IV Sent. d.47 a.2).

jhbl1q2-d1e6945.summary: Cites Averroes on De caelo as used by Thomas of Strasbourg: whatever belongs to a thing through a superior cause does not belong to it violently.
claims: What belongs to a thing through a superior cause is not violent to it.

jhbl1q2-d1e6956.summary: Applies Averroes's example of the sphere of fire moving circularly by a superior cause, neither from its own principles nor violently, to show that 'not violent, therefore natural' fails. He adds another solution: truth's illumination and the other perfections of the state of innocence are natural to us as owed (naturaliter) but not attainable from nature (a natura). They are called supernatural because nature cannot attain them, not because they are unnatural, as FitzRalph argues; more on this in Book II.
claims: Not being violent does not entail being natural from one's own principles.
The perfections of innocence are natural as owed but not attainable from nature.
'Supernatural' means not attainable by nature, not contrary to nature.

jhbl1q2-d1e6988.summary: Applies this to the argument against supernatural habits by denying that none exists. He distinguishes 'can know' by intrinsic power from 'can know' extrinsically and grants that one can know one has faith in an article. Following Brinkel, he denies that it formally follows that one knows the article to be true, since that also requires knowing that what is of faith is true. In a looser sense of 'knowing', he grants that one could know all things necessary to the merits of Christianity and sees no absurdity in this.
claims: There are supernatural habits.
Knowing one believes an article does not formally entail knowing the article is true.
In a broad sense one can know all that is necessary to Christianity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7001.summary: Answers 'there is no supernatural truth' by rejecting the premise that knowing the first principle naturally means knowing everything contained in it (Metaphysics II); the other arguments are answered by what has been said.
claims: Natural knowledge of the first principle does not yield natural knowledge of all it contains.

jhbl1q2-d1e7011.summary: Answers the objection from Hebrews 11: faith can be described in different ways according to different aspects (William of Auxerre), so the definitions need not conflict. This ends the replies on the fifth term.
claims: Different descriptions of faith capture different aspects.

jhbl1q2-d1e7023.summary: Answers the objection that the adherence of faith includes fear of the opposite by denying it; arguments for it are answered by earlier authorities.
claims: Faith does not include formido oppositi.

jhbl1q2-d1e7030.summary: Answers the objection that a first principle is more certain: the adherence of faith is the highest certitude in the sense that it belongs to the genus of highest certitude. Taking 'more' to compare a species within a genus rather than individuals within a species, he denies that a principle is more certain, and the argument does not prove it.
claims: Faith belongs to the genus of highest certitude.
First principles are not more certain than faith in kind.

jhbl1q2-d1e7044.summary: Answers the 'exceeds and is exceeded' objection: the same thing can exceed in one respect and be exceeded in another, not entitatively but denominatively, as whiteness can be a greater likeness than whiteness. This ends the replies to objections against the definitions.
claims: Faith exceeds in certitude and is exceeded in cognition without contradiction.

jhbl1q2-d1e7051.summary: Answers the objection to the first conclusion (the gospel not yet preached to all) by denying the premise, citing Romans 10 ('their sound has gone out into all the earth'). On Matthew 24, 'then' should be read not as immediately following but as successively following, meaning 'after this'.
claims: The gospel has been preached throughout the world.
'Then' in Matthew 24 means 'afterward', not 'immediately'.

jhbl1q2-d1e7063.summary: Second, with John Klenkok's postil on Acts ('it is not for you to know the times'), citing Augustine's gloss, all these signs are to be understood literally of Christ's second and final coming, to avoid exposing Scripture to ridicule.
claims: The signs in Matthew 24 refer literally to the Second Coming.

jhbl1q2-d1e7082.summary: Third, following FitzRalph (Summa de quaestionibus Armenorum VIII), the claim that the law does not bind those to whom it was not given or who are invincibly ignorant of it can be taken in two ways. In the first, they are not bound in such a way that failing to keep it makes them sin.
claims: Those invincibly ignorant of the law do not sin by failing to keep it.

jhbl1q2-d1e7091.summary: In the second way, to say they are not bound at all is false: each of them is simply bound to the law, even though failing to keep it does not put them in sin.
claims: Everyone is bound to the Christian law even if not culpable for failing to keep it.

jhbl1q2-d1e7094.summary: Concludes, with FitzRalph, that not everyone bound to a law is required to act according to it, as a murderer is bound by his judge's law without being required to carry it out. Being bound by a law differs from being required to perform it, which will be treated in Book IV on baptism.
claims: Being subject to a law differs from being required to perform it.
concepts: obligari ad legem vs. teneri facere

jhbl1q2-d1e7097.summary: Answers the second objection (infants and the invincibly ignorant) by the same distinction: it does not follow from the conclusion that everyone who fails to keep the law sins.

jhbl1q2-d1e7100.summary: Answers the third objection (unbelievers sin continuously and equally) by denying the premise: sometimes an unbeliever deviates formally and expressly from natural law and right reason and sometimes not actually. These deviations are unequal, since in the first he always sins and in the second he does not, according to some.
claims: Actual and expressed deviation from natural law differs from non-actual deviation.

jhbl1q2-d1e7105.summary: Answers the objection that the Christian law is not commensurate with divine law by denying the consequence: a lesser rule can still sometimes show a defect against a greater rule.
claims: A lesser rule can expose deviation from a greater one.

jhbl1q2-d1e7109.summary: Second, though not formally and distinctly adequate to divine law, the Christian law is proportioned to it potentially, virtually and reductively, since its rules command avoiding evil and doing good, which covers every defect of any law and every error of any sect.
claims: The Christian law is virtually adequate to divine law through the principle 'avoid evil, do good'.

jhbl1q2-d1e7112.summary: Third, the conclusion concerns laws by which people actually err, which should be called erroneous statutes of sects rather than laws, and not every possible way of erring against divine law.
claims: Erroneous sectarian rules are statutes, not laws.

jhbl1q2-d1e7118.summary: Answers the objection that the damned would continually get worse. One author ('Fastinus') grants the consequent and denies the parity with the blessed. Hiltalingen's own answer denies the consequence: the damned are continually obliged under penalty of guilt, but not under penalty of culpable worsening.
claims: The damned are obliged under penalty of guilt but do not thereby continually worsen.

jhbl1q2-d1e7126.summary: On the second objection, 'Fastinus' would grant that the damned continually sin anew but deny that they continually demerit.
claims: The damned sin anew without demerit.

jhbl1q2-d1e7132.summary: His own answer distinguishes 'sinning anew': in temporal succession of elicited acts it is true, since the damned elicit new acts at new times; but in respect of object or contempt it is false, since there is the same contempt of the same object under the same obligation, and so the same sin as to deformity and guilt, though perhaps not as to the entity of the act.
claims: The damned elicit new acts over time.
These acts constitute the same sin in deformity and guilt, not a new sin.

jhbl1q2-d1e7148.summary: Answers the objection that philosophy would be error rather than science by denying the consequence. Following Henry of Ghent, he begins a distinction: a science can be considered first in itself.
claims: Philosophy is not thereby reduced to error.
concepts: science in itself vs. in the knower

jhbl1q2-d1e7164.summary: Second, a science can be considered in relation to the knower. In the first sense, since science is properly only of the true, no science contradicts another, just as truth does not contradict truth.
claims: Science in itself is only of truths, so no science contradicts another.
