jhbl1q2-d1e7167.summary: Second, considered in relation to the knower, experts in the sciences can err and contradict one another, and through their own defect they may contradict the Christian truth. That does not make one science contrary to another, unless 'science' is taken very loosely for any writing by someone, which is neither useful nor necessary.
claims: Experts err and contradict one another, but sciences do not.
Contradiction between philosophers and the faith is due to the philosophers' error, not to science.

jhbl1q2-d1e7173.summary: Inference: Hugolino uses 'philosophical science' improperly when he means only what Aristotle wrote.
claims: Philosophy should not be identified with Aristotle's writings.

jhbl1q2-d1e7182.summary: Second inference: the principles of no science are contrary to the principles of the Christian faith.
claims: No science's principles contradict the principles of the faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e7185.summary: Third inference: Thomas Aquinas, Giles of Rome and Thomas of Strasbourg gloss Aristotle poorly when they say his arguments for the eternity of the world proceed according to natural philosophy, since then natural philosophy would contradict the faith. Aristotle argued instead from his own error and ignorance. To test this, Hiltalingen raises counter-arguments, the first being that natural science is as contrary to Christian truth as it was to Christ (gloss on 'the fortified city').
claims: Aristotle's arguments for the world's eternity reflect his own error, not natural philosophy.
Aquinas, Giles and Thomas of Strasbourg wrongly attribute those arguments to natural philosophy as such.

jhbl1q2-d1e7219.summary: Second counter-argument, from the gloss on 1 Corinthians 1 ('not in wisdom of word, lest the cross of Christ be made void'): the wisdom of the philosophers voids the cross, since nature judges it impossible for an immortal God to die, so natural science contradicts the Christian truth.
claims: Natural judgment deems it impossible that the immortal God should die.

jhbl1q2-d1e7229.summary: Third and fourth counter-arguments: by natural science one can truly judge the opposite of what the faith holds (Lazarus's resurrection, Hezekiah's sign), and Christian truth contradicts human reason, as Consentius's letter to Augustine says the heretics would not err if they trusted Scripture more than their own reasons.
claims: Natural science judges miracles impossible.
Christian truth contradicts natural reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e7261.summary: Fifth counter-argument, Holcot's: the articles of faith are not only beyond or above natural reason but against it, since natural reason concludes the opposite, as the philosophers concluded that a woman cannot conceive without a man.
claims: The articles of faith are contrary to natural reason (Holcot).

jhbl1q2-d1e7267.summary: States that these arguments can easily be answered from Henry of Ghent's conclusions noted earlier.

jhbl1q2-d1e7273.summary: Answers the first counter-argument: the gloss speaks of 'physical tradition', not 'physical science'. Following Henry, physics is the true science of natural things, while physical tradition is what philosophers have written. The first is wholly true, since God's glory fills his works; the second contradicts itself, so no wonder it contradicts us. Thus not only theology but every science is sincere truth unmixed with falsity.
claims: Physical science (true) differs from physical tradition (philosophers' writings).
Every true science is free of falsity.
Philosophers' writings contradict even each other.

jhbl1q2-d1e7295.summary: Answers the second: true wisdom does not void the cross of Christ; only what is abusively called wisdom does, as the gloss on 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise' says: God destroys not true wisdom but knowledge falsely so called, the wisdom of false philosophers that is folly before God.
claims: Only falsely named wisdom opposes the cross.

jhbl1q2-d1e7316.summary: Answers the third by granting the premise but denying that it shows a conflict with the principles of true natural science, which judge determinately only subject to the determination of the first and noblest cause, of which the natural agent (like a physician) is only an instrument.
claims: Principles of natural science hold only subject to the first cause's determination.

jhbl1q2-d1e7324.summary: Answers the fourth with Henry of Ghent: no true reason contradicts the truth of faith, though a phantasmal sophism that the ignorant take for reason may.
claims: No true reason contradicts the faith; apparent contradictions are sophisms.

jhbl1q2-d1e7332.summary: Rejects Holcot's position outright and turns his own self-objections against him to show his replies fail. First: whatever is contrary to faith is false, and what natural reason concludes is (on his view) contrary to faith, so what natural reason concludes is false.
claims: Holcot's position implies natural reason concludes falsehoods.

jhbl1q2-d1e7341.summary: Holcot's second self-objection: grace does not destroy but perfects nature, and the faith is preeminently the sect of grace, so it does not destroy nature.
claims: Grace perfects, not destroys, nature.

jhbl1q2-d1e7344.summary: Holcot's third self-objection: natural reason compels assent to what it concludes, so if it concluded the opposite of faith it would compel unbelief, which is false.
claims: If reason concluded against faith it would necessitate unbelief.

jhbl1q2-d1e7347.summary: Reports and criticizes Holcot's reply to the first: he concedes that what is contrary to faith is false and that conclusions of natural reason are often false, saying such a 'demonstration' is really a sophism, to be believed a sophism even if one cannot refute it. Hiltalingen notes that this concedes the opposite of Holcot's thesis, since no sophism is natural reason, and so his position is inconsistent and dangerous to the unlearned.
claims: Holcot's reply contradicts his own thesis.
No sophism counts as natural reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e7354.summary: Reports Holcot's reply to the second: it does not follow that what is contrary to reason does not perfect nature; rather the opposite.

jhbl1q2-d1e7358.summary: Refutes that reply: if faith is contrary to reason, the two cannot coexist in the same subject with respect to the same thing; yet if faith perfects nature, it preserves and improves it and so coexists with it. Holcot's position and reply thus entail contradictories.
claims: Contraries cannot coexist in the same subject about the same thing.
What perfects something coexists with it.

jhbl1q2-d1e7365.summary: Refutes Holcot's reply to the third (every natural reason concluding against faith must be believed a sophism): it would be both a sophism, hence false, and natural reason, hence true. He then notes that Richard of St Victor's words, that human reason protests against the Trinity, are cited in Holcot's support.
claims: Holcot's reply implies the same thing is true and false.

jhbl1q2-d1e7377.summary: First answer about Richard: for Richard 'reason protests' means the same as 'beyond reason', since in Benjamin Major he distinguishes contemplation above but not beyond reason from contemplation above and beyond reason.
claims: Richard's 'reason protests' means 'beyond reason', not 'contrary to reason'.

jhbl1q2-d1e7391.summary: Second answer: Richard means only that human argumentation cannot attain this truth of faith; elsewhere he says no one should think he can penetrate the divine light by argument, otherwise it would not be inaccessible.
claims: Richard means only that reasoning cannot reach the truths of faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e7400.summary: So Richard does not support Holcot, whose opinion Aquinas refutes in Summa contra gentiles I.7 with four reasons and Augustine's authority. The first: only falsehoods are contrary to truths, and what natural reason judges is true and faith is true, so they are not contrary.
claims: Only the false is contrary to the true.
Natural reason and faith, both true, cannot be contrary.

jhbl1q2-d1e7426.summary: Aquinas's second reason: God is the author of our natural knowledge of principles, and what a teacher instills contains the teacher's knowledge unless he teaches deceptively; so if natural knowledge contradicted faith, God's knowledge would contradict faith.
claims: God authors our natural knowledge of principles.
God does not teach deceptively.

jhbl1q2-d1e7433.summary: Third reason: contrary reasons bind the intellect and impede assent to truth, so if God were the author of a natural reason contrary to faith, God would bind us from assenting to truth.
claims: God does not impede assent to truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e7436.summary: Fourth reason: what is naturally implanted does not change while nature remains, so if it contradicted faith no one could have faith and nature together. Richard himself says God is seen differently by faith, reason and contemplation, with faith below reason in a sense. Hiltalingen concludes that natural reason is not only not contrary to faith but, in serving faith, is raised into theology above faith. This ends the replies on the first conclusion.
claims: Natural endowments are unchanging while nature remains.
Natural reason in the service of faith becomes theology, above faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e7450.summary: Answers the Augustinian objections to the second conclusion (we see our own will clearly) by granting the authority, which does not conflict. For a full answer he recalls Hugolino's modes of cognition and Hermann of Schildesche's distinction: comprehensive cognition, reaching 'that it is' and 'what it is' clearly and perfectly; and perspicuous cognition, reaching 'that it is' perfectly and in some way 'what it is', intuitively though not comprehensively.
claims: Comprehensive cognition differs from perspicuous intuitive cognition.

jhbl1q2-d1e7465.summary: The third mode reaches 'that it is' and 'what it is' not evidently but only experientially. Hermann's example is the sun, seen by the eagle in the first way, by man in the second, by the owl in the third. Hermann, Henry and Hiltalingen read the second conclusion as about the first, comprehensive mode, so Augustine's authorities do not count against it.
claims: The second conclusion denies the wayfarer comprehensive, not experiential, knowledge.
Augustine's texts about knowing one's will concern a lower mode of cognition.

jhbl1q2-d1e7480.summary: Answers the third objection (certitude of first principles): first, the consequence fails because it confuses certitude with perspicuity of evidence. Second, some, such as Giso of Cologne, would say the common axioms as usually formulated are not certain but false; for example, if a straight line can be drawn from any point to any point, one could be drawn from a point to itself.
claims: Certitude differs from perspicuity of evidence.
Common axioms as formulated admit counterexamples (Giso of Cologne).

jhbl1q2-d1e7490.summary: Likewise 'every whole is greater than its part' could be said to be falsified in a human being, a part of whom is not smaller than the whole, and similarly 'if equals are subtracted from equals the remainders are equal'.
claims: Common axioms admit theological counterexamples.

jhbl1q2-d1e7494.summary: The first counterexample to 'equals from equals' is the removal of Christ's humanity from his divinity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7497.summary: A second counterexample comes from comparing quantities along different dimensions. Hiltalingen does not adhere much to these counterexamples. He grants the consequent that a straight line can be drawn from a point to itself: first theologically, since a thing can be in several places at once.
claims: Theologically, a line can be drawn from a point to itself because of multilocation.

jhbl1q2-d1e7506.summary: Second, naturally: if a point a moves from its place toward place c while drawing the line, the line is drawn from a to a. So Giso's argument does not overturn the axiom.
claims: A moving point can trace a line from itself to itself, so the axiom is not falsified.

jhbl1q2-d1e7534.summary: Third, distinguishes argumentative from intuitive certitude: certitude reduced to that of first principles is, in the ordinary order, argumentative, not intuitive. This answers all such objections in general.
claims: Certitude by reduction to first principles is argumentative, not intuitive.

jhbl1q2-d1e7539.summary: Answers the objection from Aristotle's certitudes by denying the consequence: Aristotle could have certitude, just not the kind at issue.
claims: Aristotle had certitude, but not sincere certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e7543.summary: Second, denies the premise if 'certitude' is taken as in the conclusion: defining things is not enough; seeing them clearly and perfectly in their quantity, essence, differences and being is required.
claims: Sincere certitude requires clear vision of essence and differences, not just definition.

jhbl1q2-d1e7552.summary: Third, Aristotle's own Metaphysics II ('what is most true is the cause of truth in others') seems to point to such an exemplar, as Henry of Ghent notes. Answering the objection from Augustine, the authority is beside the point because it concerns the first truth.
claims: Aristotle acknowledged a first truth causing truth in others.

jhbl1q2-d1e7575.summary: Second, the objection rests on the false assumption that where there is no sincere simple certitude there is no truth at all, which he flatly denies.
claims: Lack of sincere certitude does not imply lack of all truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e7578.summary: Answers the objection that a science is as common as its subject: a science treating something is not enough to make it the subject; more is required.
claims: Being treated in a science does not make something its subject.

jhbl1q2-d1e7581.summary: Announces three points to clarify this: why God is the subject of theology, under what ratio, and what the object of theology is.

jhbl1q2-d1e7584.summary: On the first point, following Giles of Rome, the subject of a science is twofold: the subject in which (the knowing intellect) and the subject about which. The latter first gives the science its unity, since according to Posterior Analytics I a science is one that considers the parts and properties of one subject.
claims: A science's subject about which gives it unity.
concepts: subiectum in quo vs. de quo

jhbl1q2-d1e7607.summary: Second, the subject gives the science its distinction and diversity from other sciences.
claims: The subject distinguishes one science from another.

jhbl1q2-d1e7610.summary: Third, the subject gives the science its dignity: according to De anima I, a science of a nobler subject is nobler.
claims: A science is as noble as its subject.

jhbl1q2-d1e7620.summary: Fourth, the subject gives the science its order: the sciences are ordered as their subjects are.
claims: The order of the sciences follows the order of their subjects.

jhbl1q2-d1e7623.summary: Fifth, the subject gives the science its necessity, since diverse subjects make diverse sciences necessary and not superfluous. Giles concludes that falling under a science's consideration is not the same as being its subject.
claims: Being considered in a science is not the same as being its subject.

jhbl1q2-d1e7633.summary: Following Giles, something is considered in a science in four ways: first, per se, primarily, principally and in every way; second, per se and primarily but not in every way.

jhbl1q2-d1e7636.summary: Third, per se but not primarily.

jhbl1q2-d1e7640.summary: Fourth, neither per se nor primarily but through another. In metaphysics, being is considered in the first way, substance in the second, accident in the third. What is considered in the first way is properly the subject, and since theology considers God in that way, God is properly its subject.
claims: The subject of a science is what it considers per se, primarily and in every way.
God is properly the subject of theology.

jhbl1q2-d1e7643.summary: Concludes the first point: every modern doctor he has seen (Aquinas, 'our doctor' Giles, Henry, Scotus, Gregory, Thomas of Strasbourg) agrees that God is the subject of theology. Scotus says this is because God virtually contains all theological truths, but Gregory rightly rejects that account.
claims: All modern doctors agree that God is the subject of theology.
Scotus's account by virtual containment is rightly rejected by Gregory of Rimini.

jhbl1q2-d1e7682.summary: On the second point, under what ratio God is theology's subject, the doctors' many answers reduce to two: some posit an absolute and general ratio.
claims: Positions on the ratio of theology's subject reduce to absolute/general vs. contracted/special.

jhbl1q2-d1e7685.summary: Others posit a contracted and special ratio. Henry and Scotus hold the first view; Giles, followed by Thomas of Strasbourg, Gregory and many Augustinians, the second. Within the first, some name an attributive ratio (God as saving good, just good, etc.), others an absolute essential ratio, as Scotus does.
claims: Henry and Scotus: an absolute ratio.
Giles and the Augustinians: a contracted, special ratio.

jhbl1q2-d1e7708.summary: Notes that the second group (special ratio) also varies internally, as Giles, Scotus and others show, and refers readers there. He will now give his own view in part.

jhbl1q2-d1e7722.summary: Lays out his procedure on the ratio of theology's subject: distinctions first, then propositions, then objections and their solutions.

jhbl1q2-d1e7725.summary: First distinction: 'infinite' is taken either by the imposition of the name or by the essential perfection of what it signifies.

jhbl1q2-d1e7728.summary: Second distinction: 'infinite' is taken sometimes privatively, as excluding limitation; sometimes positively, as expressing full, interminable entity; sometimes conjointly, excluding finitude while including essential universal perfection. The last is either formal and distinct, or equivalent and interpretative.

jhbl1q2-d1e7737.summary: First proposition: the divine essence is not the subject of our theology under the ratio of infinity in the first (privative) mode, because that ratio is merely negative.
claims: Merely privative infinity cannot be the ratio of theology's subject.
A purely negative ratio is unsuitable as ratio subiecti.

jhbl1q2-d1e7740.summary: Second proof: such a ratio is not intrinsic to God.
claims: A merely privative ratio is not intrinsic to God.

jhbl1q2-d1e7743.summary: Third proof: such a ratio is not a pure perfection, so it should not be the ratio under which God is the subject of our theology, or of theology in itself.
claims: The ratio of theology's subject must be a pure perfection.
concepts: theology in itself vs. our theology

jhbl1q2-d1e7750.summary: Second proposition: under no ratio that is in no way infinite (i.e. a merely finite ratio) can God be, or is God, the subject in theology, since every such ratio is extrinsic to God.
claims: God is not the subject of theology under any merely finite ratio.

jhbl1q2-d1e7755.summary: Second proof: every such finite ratio is repugnant and opposed to God.
claims: Finite rationes are repugnant to God.

jhbl1q2-d1e7761.summary: Third proof: no such ratio is necessary, yet many parts of theology are necessary, so it cannot be their subject.
claims: Necessary theological truths require a necessary ratio subiecti.

jhbl1q2-d1e7767.summary: Third proposition: the ratio of the subject in our theology is not infinite in the second (positive, absolute) mode of the distinction.
claims: Our theology does not take God under positive absolute infinity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7770.summary: First proof: under that ratio God is known only to himself.
claims: Only God knows God under the ratio of absolute infinity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7773.summary: Second proof: that is not the ratio of the theology of the blessed, so still less of the theology of wayfarers.
claims: Even the blessed do not know God under absolute infinity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7777.summary: Third proof: that ratio concerns the simply and wholly infinite, of which no human science can exist; all commonly grant this proposition.
claims: There can be no human science of the simply infinite.

jhbl1q2-d1e7783.summary: Fourth proposition: the subject of our theology does have the ratio of the infinite.
claims: The subject of our theology has a ratio of infinity.

jhbl1q2-d1e7786.summary: Specifies that this is the third mode of the second distinction: not formally and distinctly but equivalently and interpretatively. The proof is by elimination: the subject has some ratio that is neither simply finite, nor in no way infinite, nor simply infinite.
claims: Theology's subject is infinite equivalently and interpretatively, not formally.

jhbl1q2-d1e7792.summary: Second proof: God as God is the subject of theology under an infinite, not finite, ratio, since by every confession God as such is infinite good; the antecedent is Gregory of Rimini's.
claims: God as God is infinite good.

jhbl1q2-d1e7804.summary: Third proof: God is the subject under the ratio of the true and supremely lovable (Thomas of Strasbourg), and no finite thing is supremely lovable, so the ratio is infinite in this sense.
claims: Only an infinite good is supremely lovable.

jhbl1q2-d1e7811.summary: Fourth proof: God is the subject of theology as principle of our restoration and end of our glorification (Giles), and only an infinite God can be these, as Giles shows in his treatise on God's influence on the blessed.
claims: God is theology's subject as principle of restoration and end of glorification.
Only an infinite good can save and glorify.

jhbl1q2-d1e7832.summary: Notes that Giles himself, in his treatise on the subject of theology, does not care much what the ratio is called, so long as it is contracted.
claims: Giles insists only that the ratio be contracted.

jhbl1q2-d1e7835.summary: So Peter Auriol argues more against Giles's words than against his meaning. This ends the second point.
claims: Auriol's critique misses Giles's real position.

jhbl1q2-d1e7846.summary: Draws his position: it can be held probably, indeed truly, that in every theological discourse of which God is the subject, God is subject under a ratio implying a good than which no greater can be thought.
claims: God is subject of theology under the ratio of a good than which none greater can be thought.

jhbl1q2-d1e7849.summary: Announces the third step: the arguments of these doctors and their solutions.

jhbl1q2-d1e7852.summary: Since Gregory's arguments lead to the same absurdities as those of Giles and Thomas of Strasbourg, he reports the latter. First: if God under the absolute ratio of deity were theology's subject, God would be comprehensible by our theology, since a habit with a subject under an absolute ratio must consider whatever belongs to it under that ratio (supported by Aristotle).
claims: A science with a subject under an absolute ratio considers everything belonging to it under that ratio.

jhbl1q2-d1e7876.summary: Second support: there is no reason why it would consider one thing rather than another, so it considers all.

jhbl1q2-d1e7879.summary: Third support: if it considered some things and not others, the subject would not be under an absolute ratio but a contracted one, restricted to what is considered about it as such.
claims: Selective consideration implies a contracted ratio.

jhbl1q2-d1e7882.summary: Second argument: God is not the subject of the theology of the blessed precisely as God, otherwise God would be comprehended by created knowledge, so neither of ours.
claims: God as God would be comprehended if he were subject of the blessed's theology.

jhbl1q2-d1e7890.summary: Third argument, from Giles and Thomas: our knowledge would then equal God's knowledge. These doctors try to lead the opposing view into three absurdities, the first being that our knowledge would be simply infinite.
claims: The absolute-ratio view implies our theology would be infinite.

jhbl1q2-d1e7896.summary: The second absurdity: God would be comprehended by created knowledge.

jhbl1q2-d1e7899.summary: The third absurdity: our theology would equal God's theology. With reverence, Hiltalingen argues that these absurdities follow from their own view no less than from his. Every intrinsic denomination of God is simply infinite in its kind, and every ratio they posit is intrinsic to God, so it too is infinite.
claims: Every intrinsic denomination of God is simply infinite.
The contracted-ratio view faces the same absurdities as the absolute view.

jhbl1q2-d1e7903.summary: Second counter-argument: by their reasoning, no one can consider everything that belongs to God as glorifier or as supremely lovable, so God would not be theology's subject under their ratio either.
claims: No one can consider everything belonging to God as glorifier.

jhbl1q2-d1e7906.summary: Third counter-argument: no ratio intrinsic to God is limitable or contractible, so none should be posited as contracted in God. He anticipates Thomas of Strasbourg's reply that such a ratio is partly extrinsic (by commensuration to the intellect) and partly intrinsic (taken from the thing known), and says this is insufficient.
claims: No intrinsic divine ratio is contractible.

jhbl1q2-d1e7914.summary: Rebuts Thomas's reply: such a ratio is formally God and so infinite, by their own arguments against Scotus's formal distinction. The claim that finitude is repugnant to God in being but not in understanding helps the opposing view more, since it allows an infinite God, infinitely the subject, to be known only finitely. Their position thus collapses on its own premises.
claims: Any ratio formally identical with God is infinite.
God can be infinite in being yet known finitely, which supports the absolute view.

jhbl1q2-d1e7920.summary: To clarify further, gives propositions. First: any ratio intrinsic to God can be known or theologically considered by the theologian through his theology, since any such ratio can be revealed.
claims: Every intrinsic divine ratio can be theologically known by revelation.

jhbl1q2-d1e7923.summary: Second: considering one divine ratio in theology is not incompatible with considering another; otherwise knowing more of one would mean knowing less of others.
claims: Theological knowledge of divine rationes is not mutually exclusive.

jhbl1q2-d1e7939.summary: Third: a theologian cannot consider so many intrinsic divine rationes that he could not know more; otherwise he could reach a degree of theology beyond which no progress is possible.
claims: There is no maximum to theological knowledge of God.

jhbl1q2-d1e7945.summary: Fourth: a faithful positive theologian within the bounds of this life can have infinitely many theological considerations, syncategorematically, since there are never so many that there could not be more.
claims: A wayfaring theologian can have infinitely many considerations (syncategorematically).

jhbl1q2-d1e7948.summary: Fifth: though a wayfaring theologian can have infinitely many considerations of God, it does not follow that he has infinitely many simply, or all possible ones. The first part follows from the third and fourth propositions.
claims: Syncategorematic infinity of considerations does not imply categorematic infinity or totality.

jhbl1q2-d1e7951.summary: The second part holds because otherwise the theologian would have as many considerations as God. The opponents' arguments rest on the fallacious inference from 'can have infinitely many considerations' to 'can have infinite or all considerations'. To the first argument: the theologian may consider any ratio, but not all of them.
claims: The opponents commit a fallacy from syncategorematic to categorematic infinity.
A theologian may consider any ratio, but not all of them.

jhbl1q2-d1e7954.summary: Answers the second argument: even if a theologian actually knew all God's intrinsic rationes or perfections, he still would not know God comprehensively.
claims: Knowing all divine perfections would not amount to comprehension.

jhbl1q2-d1e7957.summary: Answers the third argument by denying the consequence, which Peter Lombard would also deny (III dd.13–14 on Christ's soul's knowledge).
claims: Our theology having God as subject does not make it equal to God's knowledge.

jhbl1q2-d1e7964.summary: Draws inferences from Giles, Scotus and the preceding. First: Christ as such is not the subject of theology, since that would exclude God the Father and the Holy Spirit.
claims: Christ as such is not the subject of theology.

jhbl1q2-d1e7974.summary: Second, against Grosseteste's Hexaemeron: the ratio of theology's subject does not belong to Christ as one by a threefold unity (of supposit, of assumed nature, of mystical body or Church). Scotus holds both this and the first proposition.
claims: Christ as totus Christus is not the subject of theology (against Grosseteste).

jhbl1q2-d1e7990.summary: Third, against Hugh of St Victor (on the Celestial Hierarchy and De sacramentis prologue), as reported by Giles: the works of our restoration are not the subject of theology.
claims: The works of restoration are not the subject of theology (against Hugh).

jhbl1q2-d1e8009.summary: Fourth, against Aquinas (ST I q.1 a.1): saying simply that God is the subject of theology is insufficient. Giles holds both this and the third.
claims: Aquinas's statement that God is the subject of theology is insufficient without a specified ratio.

jhbl1q2-d1e8021.summary: Fifth, against Scotus: it is not repugnant to the ratio of this subject to be denominated through the demonstration of an attribute, since the ratio of infinity belongs intrinsically, formally and really to every attribute denomination, as will be proved later. This ends the second point.
claims: Theology's subject can be denominated by demonstrated attributes.
Infinity belongs intrinsically to every divine attribute.

jhbl1q2-d1e8029.summary: Turns to the third point, what the object of theology is, in four steps: the two most famous opinions; solving the arguments of the more modern and famous one; arguments against it; and his own conclusions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8033.summary: Presents Ockham's opinion (Prologue q.9): the subject of a science differs from its object, since the subject is the subject term of the known conclusion, while the object is what is known and immediately terminates the act of knowing, namely the known conclusion itself.
claims: For Ockham the object of science is the known conclusion.

jhbl1q2-d1e8044.summary: Restates this well-known position: the subject is that about which something is known, and the object is what is known, which is nothing other than the conclusion itself.

jhbl1q2-d1e8047.summary: Notes that Gregory of Rimini (the 'authentic doctor'), in his first article, sets out the reasons for this opinion and solves them as seems right to him and his followers.

jhbl1q2-d1e8057.summary: Presents the second opinion, Gregory of Rimini's, in three conclusions. First: the conclusion of a demonstration is not the object of the knowledge acquired through that demonstration.
claims: The conclusion of a demonstration is not the object of demonstrative knowledge (Gregory).

jhbl1q2-d1e8063.summary: Gregory's second conclusion: the external thing is not the object of science either.
claims: The external thing is not the object of science (Gregory).

jhbl1q2-d1e8066.summary: Gregory's third conclusion: the total significate of the conclusion is the object of science. Then his proof of the first conclusion: if the conclusion were the object, everyone with demonstrative knowledge would actually apprehend the conclusion, yet demonstrators usually do not reflect on the conclusion but direct attention to what it signifies. Simple apprehension of the conclusion is not science and is not caused by demonstration, and judicative apprehension that the conclusion is true is not what the geometer or physician considers.
claims: The object of science is the total significate of the conclusion (complexe significabile).
Demonstrators attend to what the conclusion signifies, not to the conclusion itself.
Neither simple nor judicative apprehension of the conclusion constitutes the science.

jhbl1q2-d1e8094.summary: Continues Gregory: knowing that the sides of a triangle are equal differs from knowing that the proposition saying so is true. The first kind of knowing is the proper, or principal, knowing of geometry and is acquired by demonstration, so its object is not the conclusion.
claims: Knowing a fact differs from knowing that the proposition expressing it is true.

jhbl1q2-d1e8097.summary: Nor is the conclusion the total object of the second kind of knowing: its object would be the proposition 'the sides are equal' is true, of which the conclusion is only a part, and that is not acquired by the same demonstration. So the conclusion of a demonstration is the object of no science acquired through it.
claims: No science has as its object the conclusion of the demonstration that produces it.

jhbl1q2-d1e8103.summary: Gregory's second main argument begins with a first supposition: 'things being so' is not the same as 'the proposition stating that they are so being true'. Aristotle (Categories, on priority) holds that although they convert, things being so causes the proposition to be true and not conversely.
claims: Being so is not identical with the proposition's being true.
The state of affairs is prior to and causes the truth of the proposition.

jhbl1q2-d1e8116.summary: Second supposition: 'things being so' is not the proposition stating it, as Aristotle says in the Categories chapter on opposites: what falls under affirmation and negation is not itself affirmation or negation, which are speech.
claims: What is signified by a proposition is not itself a proposition.

jhbl1q2-d1e8133.summary: Third supposition: a proposition is not the same as its being true; otherwise anyone apprehending the proposition would apprehend its being true.
claims: A proposition is distinct from its being true.

jhbl1q2-d1e8136.summary: Further support: the same proposition can be successively true and false.
claims: Propositions can change truth value over time.

jhbl1q2-d1e8140.summary: Applies these suppositions: the demonstration that an equilateral triangle can be constructed on any finite straight line yields knowledge of exactly that, not of the proposition's truth, which would require a different discourse and a different science. So the conclusion is not the object.
claims: Demonstrative knowledge is of what is signified, not of the truth of the conclusion.

jhbl1q2-d1e8145.summary: Confirmation: since being so differs from the proposition's being true, they are not known by the same act. What is known is not the conclusion but is signified by it, and the argument generalizes to every demonstrated conclusion.
claims: Distinct objects require distinct acts of knowing.

jhbl1q2-d1e8148.summary: Concludes Gregory's argument: the conclusion would have to be the object either of the knowledge that things are as it signifies or of the knowledge that it is true, and it is the object of neither.
claims: The conclusion of a demonstration is the object of no science.

jhbl1q2-d1e8159.summary: Gregory's proof of the second conclusion: if external things were the objects of science, many sciences such as physics and geometry would be about contingent things. Aristotle (Ethics VI; Posterior Analytics I) holds that what is known cannot be otherwise and is eternal and necessary, and everything other than God is contingent.
claims: Scientific objects must be necessary and eternal (Aristotle).
All things other than God are contingent.

jhbl1q2-d1e8185.summary: Gregory's second argument: if external things were the object of science, they would equally be the object of opinion, faith and error, so the same person would know, opine, believe and err about the same thing, for example knowing God is eternal, opining he alone moves the heavens, believing he is triune, and erring that he is finite in power.
claims: If things were objects of science, the same thing would be known, believed and erred about at once.

jhbl1q2-d1e8191.summary: Gregory's third argument: the external thing would also be the object of assent and of faith, so a believer could licitly believe the devil as firmly as God, and could assent and dissent to the same thing, all of which is absurd.
claims: Making things the objects of assent produces absurdities about believing the devil.

jhbl1q2-d1e8203.summary: Gregory's proof of the third conclusion by elimination: the object is the conclusion, the whole demonstration, the external thing, or the total significate. It is not the conclusion, nor the demonstration, nor the thing, nor the significates of all the premises (not known in one act), so it is the total significate of the conclusion.
claims: By elimination, the object of science is the total significate of the conclusion.

jhbl1q2-d1e8206.summary: Gregory's second proof: the object of science is the same as the object of scientific assent, and one assents to what the conclusion signifies. The same holds for faith and opinion: through 'God is omnipotent' the believer believes God-to-be-omnipotent. So the theological object is the total significate of a theological proposition; these are Gregory's own words.
claims: The object of science equals the object of assent.
One assents to what a proposition signifies.
The object of theology is the total significate of theological propositions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8209.summary: Hiltalingen judges that this famous opinion is not true, because of what it states, what it implies and the absurdities that follow, and because none of its arguments proves its conclusions, beginning with the first.
claims: Gregory's complexe significabile theory is false and its arguments fail.

jhbl1q2-d1e8214.summary: Answers Gregory's first argument. One reply denies the consequence because 'conclusion' is a connotative term: just as from 'he apprehends Peter, who is pope' it does not follow that 'he apprehends the pope' (as pope), so having a conclusion as object does not entail apprehending it as a conclusion.
claims: 'Conclusion' is a connotative term, so having it as object need not involve apprehending it as conclusion.

jhbl1q2-d1e8223.summary: Another reply grants that the knower actually apprehends his conclusion, and denies the inference from not thinking of it as a conclusion to not thinking of it at all, which argues invalidly from inferior to superior with a preposed negation; the converse inference is likewise invalid. Against the confirmation, the conclusion is apprehended by the same act by which it is formed.
claims: Apprehending a conclusion does not require apprehending it as a conclusion.
The conclusion is apprehended by the act that forms it.

jhbl1q2-d1e8232.summary: Does not settle whether this apprehension is simple or judicative. He rejects Gregory's claim that a judicative apprehension must be one by which the conclusion is known to be true, since the same apprehension that grasps the formation of the conclusion grasps the conclusion, and might even be the one by which it is known to conform to the thing.
claims: One act can both form the conclusion and grasp it, and perhaps grasp its truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e8241.summary: Answers the geometer and physician example: everyone has such knowledge of the conclusion, though not of it as a conclusion, which belongs to the logician (logica utens vs. docens). Against Gregory's first supposition: taken convertibly and negatively it is false; taken non-convertibly the inference from it is invalid, as shown by the analogy of being animal and being man.
claims: Considering the conclusion as conclusion belongs to logic, not to the special sciences.
Gregory's first supposition is either false or yields an invalid inference.

jhbl1q2-d1e8247.summary: Against the second supposition: 'things being so' can be taken for the dictum or for the thing signified by the dictum. In the first sense he denies it; in the second he grants it, but holds that what is so signified complexly is also signifiable by one extreme of the proposition. Aristotle's words do not support a complexe significabile distinct from things.
claims: What a dictum signifies is also signifiable incomplexly.
Aristotle does not support the complexe significabile.

jhbl1q2-d1e8258.summary: Against the third supposition: granted that a proposition is not its being true, the inference that it is therefore something else does not hold, otherwise the divine essence would differ from the Father and likeness from the like. Gregory's second argument therefore fails. He denies Gregory's second conclusion, which he thinks false and dangerous: of three options (we know only God; there are as many eternal necessary things as knowables; or we know contingent things) only the third is acceptable.
claims: A proposition's being true is not something other than the proposition.
We do have scientific knowledge of contingent things.
Gregory's second conclusion is false and dangerous.

jhbl1q2-d1e8269.summary: Answers the appeal to Aristotle: Aristotle held the opposite of Gregory on eternal significates, and following him is not a matter of faith. Better, Aristotle did not mean that the significate of a known conclusion must be necessary, otherwise no pure negative could be demonstrated, nor that every demonstration must proceed from necessary propositions.
claims: Aristotle did not require that the significates of scientific conclusions be necessary.

jhbl1q2-d1e8293.summary: Answers the second argument by granting that the external thing is the object of faith, opinion and error, and denying the absurdity: we know, believe and err about the same God under diverse rationes, relations and considerations.
claims: The same thing can be known, believed and erred about under different aspects.

jhbl1q2-d1e8301.summary: Answers the third argument by granting the first consequence and denying the further one: it follows only that one could believe some truth about the devil, whose object is the devil, as firmly as a truth about God, not that one believes the devil as one believes God.
claims: Believing a truth about the devil is not believing the devil.

jhbl1q2-d1e8305.summary: Concludes, with reverence for Gregory, that his third conclusion is badly proved and his arguments fail.
claims: Gregory's third conclusion is not proved.

jhbl1q2-d1e8308.summary: Begins the third step, arguing against Gregory's opinion first for insufficiency. If the object is the total significate, a demonstrated conclusion with no significate has no object; many propositions have none, yet there is science of negative propositions as of affirmatives.
claims: Some propositions lack significates.
There is science of negative propositions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8311.summary: Further, many propositions signify neither how things are, will be, were, nor can be. To prove that some propositions lack significates, he lays down a first supposition, granted by Gregory's followers: to be signified by a proposition is to be something, some things, or somehow.
claims: To be signified is to be aliquid, aliqua, or aliqualiter.

jhbl1q2-d1e8316.summary: Second supposition: what is wholly nothing, in any sense of being, is neither something, some things, nor somehow.

jhbl1q2-d1e8319.summary: Third supposition: whatever exists independently, uncaused and eternally is necessary.
claims: What exists independently, uncaused and eternally is necessary.

jhbl1q2-d1e8325.summary: Fourth supposition: being impossible is formally repugnant to everything necessary.

jhbl1q2-d1e8332.summary: Fifth supposition: everything that is something is either causally dependent and non-eternal or independent, uncaused and eternal, since everything is God or creature (Augustine). He then argues that 'Antichrist does not exist' is true but has no significate. Antichrist's not-existing cannot be independent and eternal, else Antichrist's existing would be impossible; and it cannot be caused, since nothing causes it, because a pure negative does not entail a positive state.
claims: Everything is either God or creature.
'Antichrist does not exist' is true but has no significate.
Non-existence has no cause.

jhbl1q2-d1e8349.summary: Second proof that 'Antichrist does not exist' is not the cause of Antichrist's non-being: if nothing existed in any way, Antichrist would not exist, yet there would be no 'it being so that Antichrist does not exist', since that would be a way of being; so the consequence fails.
claims: Non-existence can obtain with no 'being so' at all.

jhbl1q2-d1e8352.summary: Proves that no positive cause exists either: Antichrist could fail to exist even if no being were present. So Antichrist's not-being is nothing, and 'Antichrist does not exist' has no significate and the knowledge of it no object on Gregory's view. The same holds for 'a chimera is not', 'Adam was', 'Antichrist can be', as shown by 'Virbriche', Hostiensis and Klenkok. So Gregory's opinion is insufficient.
claims: Negative, past, future and modal propositions lack Gregorian significates.
Gregory's theory cannot account for knowledge of such propositions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8378.summary: Argues against the opinion's falsity and absurdity: it conflicts with the Parisian articles (condemnations), with the teaching of the saints, and with reason. First absurdity: there would have been as many things before creation as now, since for each thing there eternally was its being-possible, which is not God but a complexe significabile.
claims: Complexe significabilia would be eternal non-divine entities.
The theory conflicts with the Paris condemnations.

jhbl1q2-d1e8387.summary: Second absurdity: God could not make fewer things than there are. If God annihilated one of a hundred things, its being-annihilated would be a new thing, restoring the count to a hundred.
claims: On Gregory's theory, annihilation creates a new entity.

jhbl1q2-d1e8390.summary: Third absurdity: God could not make more things. Making a new thing a would remove the prior state of a's not-existing while adding a, so the number would not increase.
claims: On Gregory's theory, creation does not increase the number of things.

jhbl1q2-d1e8406.summary: Fourth absurdity: God could not make one thing without making infinitely many. A's existing is distinct from a (call it b), b's existing is distinct from b (c), and so on to infinity; and if b's existing is just b, then a's existing should be just a.
claims: Distinguishing a thing from its existing generates an infinite regress.

jhbl1q2-d1e8469.summary: Fifth absurdity: God could not make 'God does not create' true, since making it true would bring into being something new (its being true), which God must create. So it would always be false, contrary to Genesis's 'God rested on the seventh day'.
claims: On Gregory's theory God could never cease creating.

jhbl1q2-d1e8475.summary: Sixth absurdity: there would be infinitely many non-divine things each as intrinsically good as God, since each pure perfection belongs to God, its belonging to God is as good as the highest good, and that belonging is not God but a complexe significabile.
claims: Complexe significabilia of divine perfections would be non-divine goods equal to God.

jhbl1q2-d1e8478.summary: Clarifies that he posits several perfections, either according to explanations given elsewhere or according to others' opinions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8481.summary: Seventh argument: every complexly signifiable is incomplexly signifiable, since on their own account it is a thing or a mode of a thing, so the incomplexly signifiable would also be an object.
claims: The complexe significabile is also incomplexly signifiable.

jhbl1q2-d1e8486.summary: Eighth absurdity: the object of beatitude would be a complexe significabile rather than God, contrary to Scripture, the saints and the doctors, since the object of beatitude in hope (faith, science) in this life is the same as in the homeland. He therefore sets the opinion aside, though whatever in it serves the truth should be embraced.
claims: On Gregory's theory, God would not be the object of beatitude.
The object of beatitude is God.

jhbl1q2-d1e8495.summary: Fourth and final step, his own conclusions, prefaced by suppositions. First: to signify is for a term or intention to bring the intention of a thing to act or memory, as Aristotle's 'to signify is to establish an understanding' (Peri hermeneias) means.
claims: To signify is to bring a concept of a thing to mind.

jhbl1q2-d1e8507.summary: Second supposition: to know scientifically is to know a thing through its cause (Posterior Analytics I).
claims: Scire is to know a thing through its cause.

jhbl1q2-d1e8515.summary: Third: both signifying and knowing involve acts of the mind.
claims: Signifying and knowing concern mental acts.

jhbl1q2-d1e8521.summary: Fourth: these terms ('signify', 'know') are officiable terms.
claims: 'Signify' and 'know' are officiable terms.
'Signify' and 'know' ampliate the supposition of their terms.

jhbl1q2-d1e8527.summary: Sixth: an inference from an ampliative term to a resolvable one is not formally valid; for instance, from 'a's being is imaginable' it does not follow that a is, nor from 'Antichrist can be an animal' that Antichrist is an animal.
claims: Inferences from ampliative to non-ampliative contexts are formally invalid.

jhbl1q2-d1e8545.summary: First conclusion: a term or proposition can signify while its significate is wholly nothing, since a term can bring to mind its own concept.
claims: Signification does not require an existing significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8548.summary: Proof: the concept 'Antichrist' can be brought to mind while Antichrist is wholly nothing, so the conclusion follows from the first supposition.

jhbl1q2-d1e8551.summary: Second conclusion: one can know a conclusion while no thing at all, complex or incomplex, is signified by it, since a proposition can signify truly without an existing significate.
claims: Knowledge of a conclusion need not have an existing significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8554.summary: Third conclusion: it is impossible for a proposition to signify and not signify something, from the second supposition. Whatever signifies truly as a proposition can be known, and knowing is knowing through a cause, i.e. through some thing, so no proposition can be known without signifying something.
claims: Every known proposition signifies something.
Knowing is through some thing as cause.

jhbl1q2-d1e8560.summary: Fourth conclusion: the significate of the whole conclusion is the adequate object of the known conclusion or science, since it is what is truly signified and known through the conclusion. If the proposition itself were the object, there would be equal science of false and true propositions, since both are equally known as propositions.
claims: The adequate object of science is the significate of the whole conclusion.
If the proposition were the object, false and true propositions would be equally known.

jhbl1q2-d1e8563.summary: Fifth conclusion: 'this proposition signifies something, so something is its significate' does not follow, because of ampliation (fifth and sixth suppositions).
claims: From 'signifies something' it does not follow that some existing thing is the significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8570.summary: Sixth conclusion: 'the significate of this conclusion is something or somehow, so it is the significate of this conclusion' does not follow.

jhbl1q2-d1e8575.summary: First advantage of his position: it is sufficient, since it cannot be denied that negative propositions have an object, namely their significate.
claims: His view accounts for the objects of negative propositions.

jhbl1q2-d1e8578.summary: Second: his opinion differs from Gregory's, which always posits that the object is something or somehow, which he denies.
claims: The object of science need not be aliquid or aliqualiter.

jhbl1q2-d1e8590.summary: Third: his opinion agrees with the truth and largely with Gregory in holding that the total significate of the proposition is the object of science.
claims: The total significate of the proposition is the object of science.

jhbl1q2-d1e8593.summary: Objection to his position: it seems no different from Gregory's opinion, which it disproved, so it refutes itself.

jhbl1q2-d1e8596.summary: Objection to his first supposition (signifying as bringing a concept to mind), which seems to entail three falsehoods. First, every term would properly signify itself.

jhbl1q2-d1e8600.summary: Second falsehood: an external thing would signify terms as much as terms signify things, since the concept of a thing can bring the concept of its term to mind.

jhbl1q2-d1e8603.summary: Third falsehood: every thing would be significative of every thing, contrary to Aristotle's Peri hermeneias, which says some utterances are significative and some are not.

jhbl1q2-d1e8612.summary: Objection to the second supposition: whatever is known is known through its causes; the significate of a negative proposition is known, so it has causes, and whatever has causes exists, contrary to his position.

jhbl1q2-d1e8615.summary: Fourth objection, against his fifth and sixth conclusions: 'that no man is an ass is true', therefore 'it is true that no man is an ass', therefore 'no man being an ass' is something or somehow, since everything true is something or somehow.

jhbl1q2-d1e8620.summary: Further: what is signified by 'no man is an ass' is known, and non-being is not known (second supposition), so no man being an ass is something or somehow.

jhbl1q2-d1e8623.summary: Fifth objection: on his view a proposition could be true without things being as it signifies, contrary to Aristotle's principle that a proposition is true from the fact that the thing is or is not.

jhbl1q2-d1e8630.summary: Sixth objection: his position is insufficient, because it does not say what the significate of a proposition is: the thing, the proposition, or a complexe significabile distinct from both.

jhbl1q2-d1e8633.summary: Replies in order. To the first: his opinion differs greatly from Gregory's, first in denying, as Gregory affirms, that things are as a true pure negative proposition signifies.
claims: A true pure negative does not have an existing state of affairs as significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8636.summary: Second difference: Gregory posits the significate of every proposition as distinct from what either extreme signifies, which Hiltalingen rejects.
claims: The significate of a proposition is not distinct from what its extremes signify.

jhbl1q2-d1e8639.summary: Third difference: Gregory holds that the significates of necessary propositions are necessary and eternal, which Hiltalingen's view avoids. This answers the first objection, and the fifth and sixth suppositions answer the same argument.
claims: Significates of necessary propositions are not eternal beings.

jhbl1q2-d1e8645.summary: Introduces the answer to the second objection with the help of a Summa by 'Tholmoton' (Part 1).

jhbl1q2-d1e8653.summary: Properly speaking a term does not signify itself, though improperly it does, and that should not seem false.
claims: A term signifies itself only improperly.

jhbl1q2-d1e8657.summary: Likewise for the second and third falsehoods: improperly speaking they are granted, properly they are denied, and this is how Aristotle's distinction between significative and non-significative utterances is to be read. The same work explains why spoken and written words, rather than other qualities, are said to signify.
claims: Things and terms signify each other only improperly.
Properly, only words and writing signify.

jhbl1q2-d1e8668.summary: Answers the fourth objection with 'Firbich' (Logic): the inference from 'that-no-man-is-an-ass is true' to 'it is true that no man is an ass' (that is, that something true exists) fails, as 'a chimera is understood' does not imply that a chimera exists. Thus 'that no man is an ass is true' and 'no man being an ass is not a true thing' can both stand.
claims: Truth-predication of a dictum does not imply that an entity exists.
'A chimera is understood' does not imply that a chimera exists.

jhbl1q2-d1e8679.summary: Applies this to modals: 'that you are in Rome is possible' and 'your being in Rome is not possible' (as no existing thing) can both hold, and similarly with impossibility. This is how Aristotle's positive modal terms (Peri hermeneias II) should be understood.
claims: Modal predications of dicta do not posit entities.

jhbl1q2-d1e8688.summary: Hence the inference from 'it is not possible that you are in Rome' to 'it is impossible that you are in Rome' is to be denied in this construction. Aristotle's conversion of 'not possible' and 'impossible' applies when the modal terms are predicates (appositions) rather than subjects.
claims: Modal equivalences hold only when modal terms function as predicates.

jhbl1q2-d1e8703.summary: Answers the inference 'that no man is an ass is known, therefore it exists' by denying it. On scire per causam: Aristotle means either that the conclusion's significate is known through the conclusion as representation, with the premises' significates as quasi-causes, or that knowledge of the conclusion is caused by the premises or their habits. A doubt remains how something that does not exist can be known, since each thing relates to being known as it relates to being.
claims: Knowledge through causes means premises cause knowledge of the conclusion.
Being known does not imply existing.

jhbl1q2-d1e8716.summary: Answers the doubt: the significate of a pure negative proposition is neither something, some things, nor somehow; the same goes for propositions about the future and past whose subjects are not subjectible terms.
claims: Pure negatives and some tensed propositions have significates that are nothing.

jhbl1q2-d1e8725.summary: Clarifies that a negative proposition whose subject refers to an existing thing (e.g. 'Socrates is not in Rome') often has an existing significate and is not a pure negative (citing Anthonius's Logic). He proves that the non-existent can be known: as every sensation is cognition of a sensible object, every intellection is cognition of an intelligible object, and many things are understood that do not exist.
claims: Negatives with referring subjects are not pure negatives.
Many non-existent things are understood and thus cognized.

jhbl1q2-d1e8733.summary: On Aristotle's principle, a thing is cognizable to the extent that it is, which is true and consistent with his view.
claims: A thing is knowable in proportion to its being.

jhbl1q2-d1e8739.summary: For the remaining objections (third through sixth), he gives propositions addressing various opinions. First, against Anthonius: some true proposition that does not falsify itself has no existing principal significate, for example a true pure negative.
claims: A true non-self-falsifying proposition can lack an existing principal significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8749.summary: Second, against the same: a false non-self-falsifying proposition can be such that the significate of its contradictory does not exist, as with 'Antichrist is' and 'a chimera is'. So Anthonius's definitions of true and false propositions are defective.
claims: Anthonius's definitions of truth and falsity fail.

jhbl1q2-d1e8752.summary: Third: a proposition signifying only as things are can be false, as a self-falsifying proposition shows.
claims: Signifying only as things are does not guarantee truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e8755.summary: Fourth, against Thomas Bradwardine: a non-self-falsifying proposition that signifies as things are can still be false. Suppose a proposition signifies that God exists and that a man is an ass: it signifies as things are (God exists) and yet is false; and 'it signifies as things are' does not imply 'it signifies only as things are'.
claims: Bradwardine's definition of truth fails for conjunctive significates.

jhbl1q2-d1e8762.summary: Fifth: some affirmative and negative propositions are true without signifying precisely as things are. For affirmatives: if 'man is' signified precisely as things are, then, since 'as things are' confuses and distributes, it would signify that the heavens move and everything else, and every truth would signify every other truth's significate.
claims: True propositions do not signify precisely 'as things are'.
'As things are' distributes over all truths.

jhbl1q2-d1e8765.summary: Sixth: the significates of some propositions can fail to exist, yet those propositions cannot be false, as with 'some proposition exists' and 'some speech exists'.
claims: Some propositions cannot be false though their significates are contingent.

jhbl1q2-d1e8770.summary: Seventh: the significate of a proposition can exist and yet the proposition cannot be true while it remains. If only two propositions are written, the significate of 'only two propositions exist' obtains, yet that proposition (a third) cannot be true.
claims: A proposition's significate can obtain while the proposition cannot be true.

jhbl1q2-d1e8776.summary: Corollary: a proposition is not necessary merely because it cannot be false, nor impossible merely because it cannot be true; otherwise all such propositions would be necessary.
claims: Necessity is not equivalent to inability to be false.

jhbl1q2-d1e8779.summary: Ninth (the eighth is not numbered in the text): the significate of a proposition is not a complexe significabile distinct from the significate of one of the proposition's extremes, as all the previous arguments show.
claims: There is no complexe significabile distinct from what the extremes signify.

jhbl1q2-d1e8782.summary: Tenth: the significate of a proposition is what one of its extremes signifies. It is not the act of composition or division, otherwise without such an act God's being would not be; nor is it a complexe significabile. So God's being is God and Socrates's being is Socrates, since 'is' signifies being, which does not differ from God as a being.
claims: The significate of a proposition is the significate of an extreme.
God's being is God; Socrates's being is Socrates.

jhbl1q2-d1e8796.summary: A further argument: if God existed and nothing else did, it would be so that God exists; so by his simplicity God's being is God, and if so then, so now.
claims: By divine simplicity God's being is God.

jhbl1q2-d1e8799.summary: Opens objections to the tenth proposition: if it were true, Socrates's being would be Socrates, and the false's being would be false.

jhbl1q2-d1e8808.summary: First objection: the false's being is true, since it is known, so the false would be true.

jhbl1q2-d1e8813.summary: Second objection: then Socrates's being white would be Socrates; but something follows from 'Socrates is white' that does not follow from 'Socrates', namely that white is, so they are not the same.

jhbl1q2-d1e8835.summary: Third objection: the same thing would be known and doubted, since Socrates's being a cleric would be Socrates, and I know him to be Socrates while doubting he is a cleric.

jhbl1q2-d1e8847.summary: Fourth objection: something could make itself, since Socrates and Socrates running are the same and he can make himself run.

jhbl1q2-d1e8857.summary: Fifth objection: it would follow that what appears to be him is black, by substituting identicals.

jhbl1q2-d1e8872.summary: Sixth objection: someone who knows the proposition that signifies everything would be as wise as God, since he would know all things and that all things are.

jhbl1q2-d1e8875.summary: Seventh objection: a proposition and its subject would be convertible, since whatever one signifies the other does, which is false.

jhbl1q2-d1e8878.summary: Answers the first: 'false' is taken either for the sign of falsity or for what it signifies. In the first sense, 'the false's being is true' is granted, since it is true that it is a sign of falsity, and this is known.
claims: 'False' can mean the false sign, whose being false is true.

jhbl1q2-d1e8884.summary: In the second sense the consequence is denied: what the false sign signifies is neither true nor known in that way, and even if it were true or known, it would not follow that some false thing exists, since 'true' and 'known' are ampliative.
claims: 'True' and 'known' are ampliative and do not imply existence.

jhbl1q2-d1e8892.summary: Answers the second by denying the premise: nothing follows from 'Socrates' or 'Socrates's being' as such, but something does follow from 'Socrates is an ass' that does not follow from 'Socrates is', which is beside the point.
claims: Inference relations hold between propositions, not between terms.

jhbl1q2-d1e8908.summary: Answers the third by granting the consequent: the same thing can be known and doubted under different respects and modes of knowing.
claims: The same object can be known and doubted under different aspects.

jhbl1q2-d1e8911.summary: Answers the fourth by denying the consequence: 'Socrates can make himself run' is granted in the sense that he can produce running, but denied if taken literally as making himself.
claims: Making oneself run is producing running, not producing oneself.

jhbl1q2-d1e8925.summary: Answers the fifth by denying the consequence and its proof; what follows is only that the thing which appears to be him is, was or will be black, which is harmless.

jhbl1q2-d1e8928.summary: Answers the sixth by denying that such a knower's knowledge equals God's, since he does not know things in the way God does.
claims: Knowing all things under one proposition is not knowing them as God does.

jhbl1q2-d1e8934.summary: Answers the seventh by denying the consequence: signifying the same thing does not make terms convertible; they must also signify in the same way. The difference between a subject and a whole proposition in mode of signifying is enough to block the inference.
claims: Convertibility requires the same mode of signifying, not only the same significate.

jhbl1q2-d1e8940.summary: Concedes that his position still seems open to criticism on two counts. The first is that it has not explained the Aristotelian dictum cited against it ('from the fact that the thing is or is not...').

jhbl1q2-d1e8947.summary: The second count is that it has not shown what a necessary proposition is. On the first, following Klenkok, he reads the dictum disjunctively: a proposition is true or false from the fact that the thing is, or from the fact that the thing is not. Some truths hold because a thing is ('God is'), others because a thing is not ('Antichrist is not').
claims: Some propositions are true because something is, others because something is not.

jhbl1q2-d1e8959.summary: Supports this with Peri hermeneias I (every statement signifies that what is, is or is not, or that what is not, is or is not) and Anselm's De veritate. He then turns to the common logicians' causal reading of 'in eo quod res est' in the Categories, on which a thing's being makes present affirmatives true and its non-being makes negatives true.
claims: Every statement signifies being or non-being of what is or is not.

jhbl1q2-d1e8994.summary: Rejects that causal reading, since it makes a thing's non-being the cause of a negative's truth. In context, the Categories chapter on substance speaks of a statement becoming true or false through change in the thing, not of non-being as a cause. The chapter on priority says only that the thing is prior to and causes the truth of a true statement, not that privation or non-being causes truth.
claims: Non-being is not a cause of truth.
Aristotle's dictum concerns change in things altering truth values.

jhbl1q2-d1e9008.summary: On necessary propositions: a proposition is not necessary because its significate is something that cannot not be, otherwise pure negatives and past and future propositions could never be necessary. With 'Fibricus' he defines a necessary proposition: one that cannot be false, such that no proposition signifying whatever it signifies can be false, and whose being true is not contradicted by a proposition signifying that only it exists.
claims: Necessity is not grounded in a necessary significate.
A necessary proposition is one that neither it nor any equisignificant proposition can be false.

jhbl1q2-d1e9027.summary: Correspondingly, an impossible proposition is one that cannot be true, such that no proposition signifying whatever it signifies can be true. The clause about equisignificant propositions is needed because many contingent propositions cannot be true, or cannot be false, for reasons tied to their own existence.
claims: An impossible proposition is one that neither it nor any equisignificant proposition can be true.

jhbl1q2-d1e9030.summary: Explains why the definitions need this complexity. Some propositions cannot be true or false because their truth depends on their own existence or on something contingent required for it, such as 'this is not' (pointing to itself), 'Socrates is' (formed in Socrates's mind), or 'some proposition exists'. These are not thereby necessary or impossible, since equisignificant propositions can be true or false. The clause about non-contradiction with a proposition asserting only itself handles cases like 'no concept exists'.
claims: Self-referential propositions can be unable to be false without being necessary.
Necessity must be judged through equisignificant propositions.

jhbl1q2-d1e9070.summary: Likewise, many propositions cannot be true because of what they require, yet are not impossible, such as the opposites of those cited. None of these opposites is impossible, nor is any of the former necessary, since they depend on something contingent; so each of these propositions is contingent.
claims: Propositions that cannot be true or false due to contingent requirements are contingent.

jhbl1q2-d1e9078.summary: To identify contingent propositions he adopts the rule of Prior Analytics I: the contingent is what is not necessary and whose being posited as actual entails nothing impossible.
claims: A contingent proposition is non-necessary and its supposition entails nothing impossible.
concepts: Prior Analytics definition of the contingent

jhbl1q2-d1e9084.summary: Refers readers to the same chapter for objections and solutions, and closes the whole discussion of the object of science.

jhbl1q2-d1e9090.summary: Answers the Durandian trilemma against the third conclusion: theology should not be split into distinct creditive, defensive and elicitive habits, which would be superfluous; one habit with the other requisites suffices to elicit all such acts.
claims: Theology is a single habit, not three distinct habits.

jhbl1q2-d1e9093.summary: Second, theology is superior to faith because the same habit can extend to each of these effects.
claims: Theology's superiority lies in one habit extending to multiple effects.

jhbl1q2-d1e9096.summary: Third, if theology is a science in the first and third senses, it should also be called a science in the first sense, against Durandus, as Thomas of Strasbourg adequately proves.
claims: Theology is a science, against Durandus.

jhbl1q2-d1e9109.summary: Answers the argument that faith and theology are the same or different habits. He first reports Alphonsus's distinctions: faith is infused or acquired, and each can mean the act of believing (Augustine: faith is believing what you do not see).
claims: Faith can mean the act of believing.

jhbl1q2-d1e9124.summary: Second, faith can mean what is believed, as in the Athanasian Creed's 'this is the Catholic faith'.
claims: Faith can mean the content believed.

jhbl1q2-d1e9133.summary: Third, faith can mean that by which one believes, as in Lombard (III d.23): the virtue by which unseen things are believed. This splits further into that by which one believes subjectively (the power informed by faith) and effectively or representatively.
claims: Faith can mean the virtue by which one believes, subjectively or effectively.

jhbl1q2-d1e9139.summary: Passing over Alphonsus, whose views Thomas of Strasbourg answers, he holds that faith and theology are not the same habit. If both were uniformly diminished, some degree of the theological habit would remain but would not be called theology, since without faith it cannot denominate its possessor a theologian. So the habit can remain without faith, but theology as such cannot, at least under the present common law.
claims: Faith and theology are distinct habits.
The theological habit without faith does not count as theology under the present order.

jhbl1q2-d1e9150.summary: Corollary: being theological is not essential to the theological habit in the way being a habit is.
claims: 'Theological' is not an essential determination of the habit.

jhbl1q2-d1e9153.summary: Alternatively, faith and theology cannot be uniformly diminished in entity, knowledge and certitude, since they do not have the same range in these respects, as said in the corollaries.
claims: Faith and theology differ in range of entity, knowledge and certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e9159.summary: Answers the argument that each truth's evidence equals its certitude: first, simply deny the unproved premise.

jhbl1q2-d1e9162.summary: Second, distinguishes evidence: first, the evidence of inherence (adhesion).

jhbl1q2-d1e9165.summary: Second, the evidence of speculative cognition, which is either on the side of the thing evident or on the side of the knower. Taking evidence as adhesion, or as on the side of the thing, he grants the premise without harm to his view; taking it as speculative evidence on the side of the knower, he denies it.
claims: Evidence on the side of the thing differs from evidence on the side of the knower.
Only the knower-side evidence is unequal to certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e9168.summary: Answers the objection to the first corollary (faith as certain as demonstration): first, simply deny the antecedent.

jhbl1q2-d1e9171.summary: Second, distinguish certitude of adhesion from certitude of cognition, as before.

jhbl1q2-d1e9174.summary: Third, certitude is either on the side of the thing known or on the side of the knower. Though faith may lack equal certitude on the side of the knower, it has equal certitude on the side of the thing, which suffices for the corollary.
claims: Faith equals demonstration in object-side certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e9178.summary: Answers the objection that faith would be finite and infinite: 'infinite' is taken properly, for an infinite entity in genus or species.

jhbl1q2-d1e9181.summary: Or improperly, by extrinsic or intrinsic denomination: the soul is finite in essence but infinite in capacity ('Clineton'), and a morally bad act is finitely bad yet said to be infinitely so (Randolph of Castello, 'Fastinus' of Asti). So a finite knowledge can be an infinite certitude. Alternatively, deny that an infinite knowledge-thing is therefore an infinite thing.
claims: Something finite in being can be called infinite by denomination.
Faith can be finite knowledge yet infinite certitude.

jhbl1q2-d1e9195.summary: Answers Brinkel's first argument against the third corollary: denies its premise, holding that the light of faith together with the free command of the will suffices, without other evidence, to cause assent to a non-evident proposition.
claims: Faith plus free command of the will suffices for assent without further evidence.

jhbl1q2-d1e9201.summary: Second, the argument does not prove its point: even if faith cannot cause assent without discourse, it has not been shown that faith does not suffice to cause that discourse and so the assent.
claims: Faith may itself cause the discourse needed for assent.

jhbl1q2-d1e9204.summary: Third, the major premise can be read two ways. If the required discourse is extrinsic to faith, of a higher degree of evidence, the major is false, as the experience of many unlearned believers shows.
claims: Unlearned believers assent without extrinsic rational discourse.

jhbl1q2-d1e9207.summary: If the discourse is faith's own effect, a kind of weak knowledge or evidence, he grants the major but denies the minor, since every proposition faith inclines to is in some way evident and known to the believer.
claims: Every proposition of faith is in some way evident to the believer through faith itself.

jhbl1q2-d1e9214.summary: Notes, first, that Holcot (I q.9 a.1) speaks of someone without the habit of faith who hears a preacher and asks whether he can freely assent at once without rational evidence, and Holcot answers no. Hiltalingen, by contrast, speaks of someone who has infused faith.
claims: Holcot's case concerns someone without infused faith; Hiltalingen's concerns someone with it.

jhbl1q2-d1e9227.summary: Second, Holcot's conclusion is either pointless or smacks of heresy. If he means that rational evidence without faith suffices to believe all the articles, that is unsound; if he means that without faith the will alone cannot assent, that is true, but he assigns the wrong cause, lack of rational evidence rather than lack of faith.
claims: Holcot's view is either heretical or misattributes the cause of non-assent.

jhbl1q2-d1e9233.summary: Answers Brinkel's second argument (simple believers dissent from some article). He denies the minor, saying one can have faith regarding the article without having faith in it in that respect, like 'I know the pope runs' without 'I know of the runner that he is pope'. Alternatively, he distinguishes specific explicit faith from general confused implicit faith: with the first, the major is true and the minor false.
claims: Explicit faith excludes dissent; implicit faith can coexist with material error.

jhbl1q2-d1e9243.summary: With general implicit faith, the major is false and the minor true. Or: if 'per se and immediately' excludes everything other than faith, even faith's own effects, he grants both reasons and conclusion, but this is beside the point. If it excludes only further and more eminent evidence, the arguments fail.
claims: Read strictly, 'per se and immediately' makes Brinkel's conclusion trivially true.

jhbl1q2-d1e9251.summary: Brinkel's reasons assume the first reading and his conclusion the second, so the conclusion is not well proved.
claims: Brinkel equivocates between two senses of 'immediately'.

jhbl1q2-d1e9254.summary: Answers Brinkel's third argument (infused faith yields no assent) by denying the consequence in the intended sense: by parity, no habit would suffice per se to cause its act, since its effect does not follow at once. If 'per se' excludes everything not faith, the argument holds trivially, since assent also requires the power, the act and the discourse, none of which is the habit. This ends the third conclusion.
claims: Habits suffice for their acts though other requisites are needed.
Assent requires the power, act and discourse besides the habit.

jhbl1q2-d1e9262.summary: Turns to the objections against the fourth conclusion, answering briefly since the doctors already named answer them well.

jhbl1q2-d1e9265.summary: Answers the first Marchian argument by denying that the knowledge of Christianity is self-evident to the knower, and denying that one is bound to believe only what is self-evident, a view condemned as error at Paris (art. 3), unless 'self-evident' is taken very broadly as in William of Auxerre (nothing more known to believers than the articles). Even then 'more certain' would fit better, and this is not Marchia's meaning. Distinctions of 'per se notum' in Hugolino and John 'de Braculis' are noted.
claims: The articles of faith are not self-evident to the knower.
