The view that only what is self-evident should be believed was condemned at Paris.

jhbl1q2-d1e9297.summary: Answers the second (per se false and per se true are equally indubitable): the major is false, since the power perceiving truth and falsity may relate differently to each, often judging the true to be false. Alternatively, distinguish dictum and thing; or, against the minor, the truths of faith, though true in themselves, are not as known to us under the common law as they are true in themselves.
claims: Truths of faith are not as evident to us as they are true in themselves.

jhbl1q2-d1e9300.summary: Answers the third (regress) argument by granting that there are first believed principles. They are believed neither because of something self-evident nor because of another belief, but through the habit of faith, the command of the will, and the authority of the speaker. As Augustine says, what we know we owe to reason, what we believe to authority, and Christ gives infallible truth about eternal things.
claims: First articles are believed on authority, through the habit of faith and the will.
What we know we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority.

jhbl1q2-d1e9333.summary: Answers the objection from Mark, Matthew and the Athanasian Creed to the first corollary: first, these texts apply to those who have and use reason.
claims: The requirement of faith for salvation applies to those with use of reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e9345.summary: Second, they take the act for the habit ('whoever does not believe' means whoever lacks faith); or third, 'does not believe' means 'refuses to believe'.
claims: 'Not believing' in these texts means lacking the habit or refusing to believe.

jhbl1q2-d1e9349.summary: Answers the second (the child of another sect at the age of reason): if he believes his sect and knows or can know it deviates from the Christian law, the argument fails. If he cannot, but his inability stems from his own fault or from imputed fault such as original sin, it does not excuse him, as Anselm says (Cur Deus homo I.24): whoever does not render God his due is unjust, even if he cannot.
claims: Inability due to original sin does not excuse.
Whoever does not render what is due to God is unjust, even if unable.

jhbl1q2-d1e9376.summary: Answers the third (all must believe as Rome believes) by granting the antecedent and denying the consequence: conformity of members to the Church consists not in believing as it believes but in believing as it commands to be believed.
claims: Members must believe what the Church commands, not everything the Church believes.

jhbl1q2-d1e9379.summary: Turns to objections against the fifth conclusion, noting first a distinction: it is one thing to say a sensible miracle suffices to cause perfect intuitive knowledge in the sense of the second conclusion.

jhbl1q2-d1e9382.summary: Another to say it suffices to cause evident scientia, and another again to say it suffices to cause true faith.
claims: Miracles may cause faith without causing evident science.

jhbl1q2-d1e9387.summary: So says Bradwardine (De causa Dei I.1): arguments from miracles do not give a mathematical demonstration concluding from self-evident principles.
claims: Arguments from miracles are not mathematical demonstrations.

jhbl1q2-d1e9400.summary: Second, if things can be otherwise than they appear to any sensation, this is either by a finite power, which is false (no finite power could make the world not larger than me or a star not smaller than the heavens), or by God's infinite power alone. Anyone positing that must believe before understanding, so Brinkel's arguments presuppose faith in God's free infinite power and do not prove their conclusion.
claims: Only infinite power could make sensory appearances systematically deceptive.
Brinkel's skeptical arguments presuppose faith in divine omnipotence.

jhbl1q2-d1e9407.summary: Confirms the fifth conclusion. First: Peter often heard Christ reveal the secrets of his heart (affections, thoughts, inner speech) determinately and distinctly; no finite power can do this, so through such miracles Peter could know Christ to be God.
claims: Revealing the secrets of hearts requires infinite power.
Peter could know Christ's divinity from such miracles.

jhbl1q2-d1e9419.summary: Second: Christ could reveal to Peter all future events of the world, including those depending on human free will, which no finite power can do. The objection from prophets is easily answered: they do not know by their own power, while Christ acted, and said he acted, by his own power or that of the Father, with whom he is one.
claims: Foreknowing free future contingents requires infinite power.
Prophets know by God's power; Christ by his own.

jhbl1q2-d1e9433.summary: Third: Christ said he did these miracles by his own power or the Father's. Either this was true, which gives the conclusion, or he was a liar until death and so damned, which Christians and metaphysicians alike reject. Moreover, the apostles and saints would not then have worked the miracles after his death that the whole world attests.
claims: Christ was either truthful about his divine power or a damned liar.
Post-resurrection miracles of the apostles confirm Christ's claims.

jhbl1q2-d1e9439.summary: Answers Brinkel's first argument by granting that sensible signs suffice and judging the opposite to derogate from Christ's words. He denies the major (if sense can err through one sensation it can err through any): otherwise, through the very sensation by which I feel pain I could judge it not pain, and feel myself healthy and sick, hot and cold.
claims: Not every sensation can be erroneous.
Denying the probative force of signs derogates from Christ's words.

jhbl1q2-d1e9454.summary: Second, the major concerns either a finite or an infinite agent: if finite it is false, and if infinite the intended conclusion does not follow.

jhbl1q2-d1e9457.summary: Third, none of Brinkel's arguments proves his conclusion, because the sensory errors he cites concern only things subject to natural, finite powers. Extending this to sensible events that only infinite power can produce is invalid; more on this at the beginning.
claims: Sensory error concerns natural phenomena, not miracles requiring infinite power.

jhbl1q2-d1e9469.summary: Defers further treatment to Book III, where it will be asked whether the promised Messiah can truly be proved to be the natural Son of God.

jhbl1q2-d1e9478.summary: Answers the objection that some things must be understood before they are believed, with William of Auxerre: some things, such as that there is one principle, must be understood by natural cognition before being believed, while others, the articles of faith, must be believed before they are known.
claims: Some truths (e.g. one first principle) are understood before believed; articles of faith are believed before known.

jhbl1q2-d1e9486.summary: So the authority does not oppose the conclusion: from being able to understand some truths of the faith it does not follow that one can understand the whole faith.
claims: Understanding some truths of faith does not imply understanding all.

jhbl1q2-d1e9495.summary: Clarifies that the fifth conclusion concerns not a single conclusion but the whole truth of the Christian faith necessary for salvation.
claims: The fifth conclusion concerns the totality of saving truth.

jhbl1q2-d1e9498.summary: Answers the astrological objection by flatly rejecting Albumasar: no constellation suffices to begin or distinguish any religion, and Christians should not assert such predictions about matters that depend on free will, as Augustine teaches in several books.
claims: No constellation suffices to cause a religion.
Astrological predictions about free acts should not be asserted.

jhbl1q2-d1e9515.summary: Answers the objection to the first corollary (Scripture over reason) with propositions. First: believing something true can merit eternal death, as when someone foreknown to damnation believes that God will finally not have mercy on him, and so sins mortally by despair.
claims: Believing a true proposition can be mortally sinful (despair).

jhbl1q2-d1e9519.summary: Second: in some cases a falsehood should be believed more than its true opposite, as the foreknown should believe God will have mercy on him even though the opposite is true.
claims: In some cases one ought to believe a falsehood rather than its true opposite.

jhbl1q2-d1e9524.summary: Third: some act merits eternal death and yet cannot be committed knowingly, as when a predestined person believes that God will not have mercy on him: he errs, and he cannot know that he errs in so believing, since then he would both err and not err.
claims: Some damnable acts cannot be committed knowingly.

jhbl1q2-d1e9533.summary: Fourth: in some cases one could licitly disbelieve a word of Christ, of the Church, or of Scripture, as a foreknown person to whom any of these announced his final damnation.
claims: One may licitly disbelieve a revelation of one's own damnation.

jhbl1q2-d1e9539.summary: So Peter licitly disbelieved Christ's 'you will deny me three times', though this does not mean Christ could lie; such a person should take the revelation as conditional, or himself as not grasping the speaker's intention (treated in Book I d.40). With Henry of Ghent he distinguishes authority (which seeks faith) from reason (which forms understanding): as to the thing believed, Scripture is simply to be relied on more; as to the believer, it depends whether reason persuades evidently or only probably.
claims: Peter licitly disbelieved Christ's prediction.
Authority demands faith; reason forms understanding.
As to the thing believed, Scripture outweighs reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e9568.summary: Completes Henry's distinctions: where reason persuades only probably, Scripture (canonical or of similar authority) is to be believed more. Where Scripture and reason do not conflict but agree, one should believe more because of Scripture if Scripture persuades sufficiently, and more because of reason if it does not.
claims: Against merely probable reason, canonical Scripture prevails.
Where both agree, weight follows the sufficiency of persuasion.

jhbl1q2-d1e9571.summary: Concludes that, simply speaking, Scripture is to be relied on more than natural reason, with Augustine (Super Genesim): the authority of Scripture is greater than all the perspicacity of human genius.
claims: Simply speaking, Scripture is to be relied on more than natural reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e9583.summary: Answers the objection directly: a word of Christ spoken to an individual need not be relied on by that person as much as Scripture simply, especially in the sense he takes it.
claims: A private word to an individual differs from Scripture in its claim to reliance.

jhbl1q2-d1e9586.summary: Alternatively, the minor premise can be denied.

jhbl1q2-d1e9589.summary: Or the form is invalid: if the premises are true they are particular, or the minor is not properly subsumed under the major. This answers the whole argument.
claims: The objection's syllogism is formally invalid.

jhbl1q2-d1e9592.summary: Answers Giles's argument against the second corollary (clear vision necessitates love). First, deny the antecedent: Anselm's authority concerns necessity of coercion, which opposes freedom of complacency, not necessity of inevitability, which opposes only freedom of contradiction and contingency. Or, following Buckingham(?), Roseth and Bonsembiante, there are two kinds of acts of the will, the first being willing and nilling.
claims: Coercive necessity differs from necessity of inevitability.
Clear vision may necessitate love without destroying freedom of complacency.

jhbl1q2-d1e9609.summary: The second kind of will-acts are consequent appetites like rejoicing and sorrowing. Anselm's authority concerns the first kind, not the second, in which the will can be necessitated since it undergoes them more than it does them.
claims: The will can be necessitated in passive consequent acts such as joy.

jhbl1q2-d1e9615.summary: Third, perhaps better: from 'he necessarily loves while such vision remains' it does not follow that he necessarily loves, since the vision does not necessarily remain in the seer; this argues invalidly from inferior to superior with negation.
claims: Conditional necessity of love does not imply absolute necessity.

jhbl1q2-d1e9622.summary: Fourth, necessity of love and the condition of a wayfarer are not mutually exclusive, as in Christ and others confirmed in grace.
claims: Being a wayfarer is compatible with necessitated love (as in Christ).

jhbl1q2-d1e9625.summary: Turns finally to the principal arguments, all of which oppose the third corollary of the fifth conclusion (that without illumination and faith the truth of Christianity cannot be known), beginning with the first.

jhbl1q2-d1e9628.summary: Answers the first principal argument: he grants, in Henry's sense, that the intellect can naturally know something, but denies with Henry that it is equally apt from the outset to know every truth, and denies the analogy with sense, for reasons Henry gives.
claims: The intellect is not equally apt to know every truth from the outset.

jhbl1q2-d1e9641.summary: Answers the second supporting argument by denial: knowables do not share the same ratio in the same way, and the whole ratio of understanding lies not only in the truth but also in the intellect.
claims: The ratio of understanding involves the intellect as well as the truth known.

jhbl1q2-d1e9646.summary: Answers the third supporting argument (from ens commune) with Scotus's response in his first prologue question: the consequence is to be denied.
claims: Natural perception of common being does not yield knowledge of every being.

jhbl1q2-d1e9659.summary: Answers the second principal argument (the damned and demons know): whatever of the antecedent, the consequence is denied. The agent-patient principle holds of a total agent, and the agent intellect is not the total cause of intellection.
claims: The agent intellect is not the total cause of intellection.

jhbl1q2-d1e9666.summary: Answers the third principal argument: illumination is required both as elevating and as assimilating. A finite elevation sufficiently removes the disproportion, either because even an infinite disproportion can be removed by finite elevation, or because the disproportion is only finite.
claims: Illumination elevates and assimilates.
Finite elevation suffices to remove the disproportion.

jhbl1q2-d1e9681.summary: Denies that natural reason could be intensified enough to remove the resistance, and grants that a finite resistance can impede infinitely: in a proportion of equality, any small resistance removed lets action follow, but while equality stands no natural agent can act. So illumination is required as elevating.
claims: A finite resistance can block action indefinitely in a proportion of equality.
Natural reason cannot be intensified to supply illumination.

jhbl1q2-d1e9684.summary: Answers the second sub-argument: elevation is considered in certitude or in cognition. In certitude, faith with illumination elevates equally or more than reason. The inference that Christianity then depends more on faith than on reason can be denied, since reason and its use are presupposed by actual faith.
claims: In certitude faith with illumination elevates at least as much as reason.
Reason is presupposed to actual faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e9699.summary: Or the consequent can be granted as unproblematic and conformed to Scripture; Brinkel's reasons against it fail, as the third conclusion and its corollaries show.
claims: Christian truth may depend more on faith than on reason.

jhbl1q2-d1e9705.summary: If elevation is considered in evidence and cognition, illumination elevates more than faith, per the third conclusion. That it would then be science is granted in a broad sense, but it does not follow that it cannot coexist with faith; Hugolino answers the contrary arguments.
claims: Illumination exceeds faith in evidence.
Broadly speaking, theological science can coexist with faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e9714.summary: Alternatively, illumination is required as assimilating. What the assimilation is follows from the fourth term: in one sense it is God, as many authorities in John 'de Braculis' and Augustine show (City of God VIII.7: the light of minds is the one who made all; Contra Faustum: that light is the inseparable Trinity, one God).
claims: In one sense the assimilating illumination is God himself.

jhbl1q2-d1e9745.summary: In the second sense, illumination is the motion of the power so illuminated or elevated.

jhbl1q2-d1e9748.summary: In the third, it is the act of the power together with the object and the illuminating principle. Against 'then everyone so illuminated would be blessed', the consequence fails.
claims: Having God as illuminating principle does not make one blessed.

jhbl1q2-d1e9753.summary: Answers 'everyone would know in the Word' by distinguishing: the Word can be the ratio of knowing in any way whatsoever, and in this sense he grants it; or it can be the clear, naked, intuitive ratio of knowing and also the primary object, and in this sense he denies it.
claims: Knowing through the Word as ratio differs from knowing the Word as primary object.

jhbl1q2-d1e9759.summary: This distinction is drawn from Henry of Ghent (Summa a.1 q.2).

jhbl1q2-d1e9766.summary: John 'de Brakil' would answer differently: no intellect, divine or created, understands anything with 'evening knowledge' as known precisely in itself and not in the eternal Word, since every intellectual striving comes to rest only in the Word. So the Word is not only ratio but also term and object of cognition, and he grants that both good and bad can intuit God's face in this life, distinguishing first that 'face' means a thing's power by which it shows itself.
claims: No intellect comes to rest except in the eternal Word (Brakil).
Good and bad alike can in some sense see God's face in this life (Brakil).

jhbl1q2-d1e9781.summary: In the second, strict sense, a thing's 'face' is its most proper and distinguishing radiance, by which it is known as distinct from all else; in this sense only certain beings properly have faces.

jhbl1q2-d1e9790.summary: Brakil's conclusion is to be read of the first sense of 'face', consistent with his claim that no rational being knows anything intuitively except God. But since he uses the term loosely and improperly, Hiltalingen stays with his first answer.
claims: Brakil uses 'intuitive' loosely; the first answer is preferred.

jhbl1q2-d1e9802.summary: Turns to the third sub-objection: the nearer to God, the nearer to this assimilation.

jhbl1q2-d1e9805.summary: The consequent can be granted, but it does not follow that the nearer one is the wiser unless the assimilation is more intense; or, real proximity does not suffice, only immutative or objective proximity does.
claims: Wisdom tracks intensity of assimilation, not mere proximity.
Real proximity differs from objective proximity.

jhbl1q2-d1e9808.summary: Answers the fourth: this assimilation does not work by inherence.
claims: Assimilating illumination is not inherent in the soul.

jhbl1q2-d1e9811.summary: Answers the fifth: it does not follow that God must inform the intellect of all forms at once, since God freely moves and changes the power not only terminatively or immutatively but also objectively. Hence several claims of John of Marchia and Richard 'Barbe' rest on a falsehood, as will be shown at d.12. This completes the third principal argument.
claims: God freely selects what he makes known by illumination.

jhbl1q2-d1e9826.summary: Answers the fourth principal argument by granting that such a light is infused into all theologians. Against Alphonsus's inference from moderns not perceiving it, the consequence is denied: Henry's 'those who receive perceive' does not imply 'those who do not perceive do not receive'.
claims: All theologians receive the light.
Not perceiving does not imply not receiving.

jhbl1q2-d1e9838.summary: Alternatively, all moderns do perceive it, but not perfectly, nor do they perceive that they perceive it, and so they deny it.
claims: One can perceive something without perceiving that one perceives it.

jhbl1q2-d1e9841.summary: Third, a parallel argument would prove there is no infused habit of charity or created grace, since not all who have them perceive them.
claims: The argument would disprove infused charity and grace.

jhbl1q2-d1e9846.summary: Fourth, Hugh of St Victor (De anima Christi): the light shines and illuminates, but not all who see by it see it.
claims: One can see by a light without seeing the light.

jhbl1q2-d1e9856.summary: Answers the second sub-argument (theologians can freely dissent) by denying the consequence.
claims: Capacity to dissent does not exclude illumination.

jhbl1q2-d1e9859.summary: Answers the third (theologians would adhere more firmly): the consequence fails, since faith equals the theologian's adhesion in firmness, though not in cognition or knowledge.
claims: Simple faith and theology are equal in firmness, unequal in cognition.

jhbl1q2-d1e9863.summary: Answers the fourth (faith would not be necessary for theologians) by denying the consequence, from what was said.
claims: Theologians still need faith.

jhbl1q2-d1e9866.summary: Answers the fifth (noble habits cannot be hidden): it is clear how illumination is hidden from us and how not, and the argument is formally invalid.
claims: Illumination is in some respects hidden from its possessor.

jhbl1q2-d1e9869.summary: Answers the sixth (one spiritual light suffices) by denying the consequence, since natural and supernatural light are not alike. Alternatively, even in the natural order the natural light does not suffice alone but many habits are needed, and likewise in the supernatural order illumination is needed.
claims: Even natural knowledge requires many habits beyond the natural light.

jhbl1q2-d1e9872.summary: Answers the seventh: illumination is intermediate between faith and glory by formal negation and by virtual participation. This completes the fourth principal argument.
claims: Illumination mediates between faith and glory by formal negation and virtual participation.

jhbl1q2-d1e9875.summary: Answers the fifth principal argument (reason can prove a future life): the consequence can be denied, since even if reason can infer some future life, it cannot do so in the manner or with the perfection the Christian truth affirms.
claims: Natural reason cannot know the future life as Christian faith teaches it.

jhbl1q2-d1e9881.summary: Alternatively, the premise can be denied and its proofs rejected, since similar reasoning would prove that man can attain final salvation and perfect beatitude from purely natural powers, which is false. This answers all the arguments, and the question ends.
claims: Man cannot attain final beatitude from purely natural powers.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e128.summary: First principal argument against the thesis. Drawing on Henry of Ghent and Scotus, it argues that the intellect, as a natural power, attains every intelligible truth by its own nature, equally and from the outset, like sense toward sensibles: all intelligibles share one ratio of acting on the intellect, and a power that reaches common being reaches everything under it, including the divine. Special illumination is therefore unnecessary.
claims: The intellect as a natural power can attain its natural object without special illumination.
The intellect is equally apt to know every intelligible truth.
Natural attainment of ens commune extends to every being, including God.

jhbl1q2-Dssdeqf.summary: Second principal argument against the thesis: those who lack faith and grace, such as the damned (the rich man of Luke 16), a damned heretic, and demons, can know the truth of the faith. Since the agent and possible intellects are equally disposed in humans and angels, a wayfarer too can know it by natural reason (Michael of Massa, via Alphonsus).
claims: The damned and demons know the truth of the faith without special illumination.
Equal disposition of agent and patient yields equal action.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e243.summary: Third principal argument against the thesis, a dilemma over how special illumination would work. As elevating, it would be either finite (insufficient for an infinite object) or infinite (impossible, since even the light of glory is finite); it would also be superfluous or would make theology depend more on faith than on reason, and it would amount to scientia incompatible with faith. As assimilating, if it were God it would make its possessors blessed, give them cognition in the Word, make God inhere in creatures, and impress all exemplar forms at once; if it were a creature, its own defenders would be contradicted.
claims: Special illumination cannot coherently be either elevating or assimilating.
If illumination exceeded faith it would be science and exclude faith.
Identifying illumination with God entails absurdities such as beatitude and divine inherence.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e364.summary: Fourth principal argument against the thesis: if the thesis were true every theologian would receive a special light, but modern theologians do not perceive it (Alphonsus, applying Henry's principle that recipients perceive). Six supporting reasons follow: theologians can freely dissent, they would assent more firmly than simple believers, their faith would cease to be faith, noble habits cannot stay hidden (Thomas of Strasbourg), one spiritual light suffices as one natural light does, and the illumination cannot be intermediate between faith and glory.
claims: Theologians do not perceive any special light and so do not have one.
Evidence would remove the freedom to dissent.
Special illumination would be incompatible with theologians' faith.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e436.summary: Fifth principal argument against the thesis: natural reason can demonstrate a future life, which is an article of Christianity, from humanity's natural ordering to a final rest that nothing in this life provides (with Augustine's 'restless heart'). Anselm's threefold course of things and Hugh of St Victor's account of natural knowledge of the invisible God are added in support.
claims: Natural reason can prove a future life.
Some knowledge of the invisible God is available by nature.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e536.summary: First argument for the opposite: a set of authorities, namely 1 and 2 Corinthians, Augustine on Genesis, De sermone Domini and City of God, Ambrose, and Peter Lombard. Together they teach that the wisdom of the faith exceeds human reason, that whatever truth reason grasps is due to the divine light, and that every truth comes from the Holy Spirit.
claims: The wisdom of faith exceeds human comprehension.
Truth grasped by reason is owed to the divine light of truth.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e735.summary: Second argument for the opposite, from Augustine: no one becomes better or wise by human reason alone.
claims: Wisdom is not attained by human reason alone.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e759.summary: Third argument for the opposite, from Augustine's 83 Questions: created wisdom comes only through illumination by God's grace, which nearly restates the question.
claims: Created wisdom requires divine illumination.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e795.summary: Fourth argument for the opposite: believing must precede knowing the truth of the faith (Augustine, Richard of St Victor, cited by Hugolino).
claims: Faith precedes understanding.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e882.summary: Fifth argument for the opposite: humans cannot distinctly know their ultimate end without faith and special illumination, as Scotus argues against the philosophers, and the truth of the faith chiefly concerns that end.
claims: The ultimate end is not distinctly knowable by natural reason.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1238.summary: Defines 'truth' in three senses: incomplex (truth as being, or as God), complex (the total significate of a proposition, Gregory's and Hugolino's complexe significabile, also in Anselm), and truth as the sign of truth (a true proposition, true and false being in the intellect).
claims: 'Truth' is said incomplexly, complexly, and of propositions as signs.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1341.summary: Defines the 'Christian sect' as the congregation of the faithful obediently united under the rite and precepts of Christ their principal shepherd. Its rite varies as precepts, counsels and sacraments, and 'sect' need not carry a negative sense.
claims: The Christian sect is the congregation of the faithful under Christ.
'Secta' is not necessarily pejorative.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1394.summary: Defines 'reason': as the higher part of the soul bearing God's image, and as a medium making an unknown proposition known. Hiltalingen rejects Brinkel's definition (the abstractive medium) as both too broad and too narrow, and proposes his own: what by its nature immediately suffices to cause knowledge of an unknown proposition, abstractively or deductively. He supplements it with Cassiodorus, Augustine and William of St Thierry, distinguishing ratiocination (seeking) from reason (finding).
claims: Ratio can mean the image-bearing higher soul or a medium of knowing.
Brinkel's definition of ratio is inadequate.
Reason is what naturally suffices to cause knowledge of an unknown proposition abstractively or deductively.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1543.summary: Defines 'illumination' in three senses: the assisting illuminating principle (Augustine's eternal truth present to the mind), the motion by which the illuminated power is moved toward its object, and the act produced through that motion and assistance.
claims: Illumination can be the illuminating principle, the cognitive motion, or the resulting act.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1613.summary: Defines 'faith': Brinkel's definition as a supernaturally infused habit elevating the intellect to supernatural truths, then Hostiensis's canonistic senses (baptism, marital fidelity, pledged security, conscience, credulity, the collection of articles). Hebrews 11 is judged insufficient as a definition. Against the formula 'below science, above opinion', Hiltalingen insists that faith is below science only in evidence, not in certitude of adhesion.
claims: 'Fides' is equivocal across theological and legal uses.
Hebrews 11:1 is a description, not a definition.
Faith equals or exceeds science in certitude while falling below it in evidence.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1743.summary: Defines the 'adherence of faith', with Hugolino, as the greatest certitude a wayfarer has, adhering to what is not evident but believed to be revealed by the First Truth, supported by Hugh of St Victor's definitions read as concerning evidence. This ends the second article.
claims: Adherence of faith is the wayfarer's greatest certitude, grounded in revelation, not evidence.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1795.summary: First conclusion: the Christian law binds every rational creature and condemns every erroneous sect. It is proved from the love commandments, the eternal law (Cicero), the great commission, and Augustine's De doctrina christiana. The corollaries: the damned remain bound to will justly, a damned angel is obliged to give up its evil will though unable to, and every doctrine contrary to the Christian law is error. The truth of Christianity is thus 'sincere', unmixed with falsity.
claims: The Christian law obliges every rational creature.
The damned remain under obligation even when unable to comply.
Whatever contradicts the Christian law is error, since truth cannot contradict truth.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e1890.summary: Second conclusion: under the present order no wayfarer perfectly and intuitively knows any sincere truth, since wayfarers lack intuition of specific and individual differences and of substances (the Eucharist), and the light of the agent intellect is phantasm-bound. Yet theology knows its objects more perfectly than any other created science, because it knows them as ideally represented in the triune God and freely produced. Supported by Hermann of Schildesche and Hugolino's five grades of cognition, the corollaries defend Henry of Ghent's doctrine of the eternal exemplar against misreadings and, with Giles, affirm that theology is maximally unified yet treats all things.
claims: Wayfarers lack perfect intuitive knowledge of any sincere truth.
Theology knows things more perfectly than other sciences by knowing them in God.
Sincere certitude requires the eternal exemplar, though error-free certitude does not.
Henry of Ghent has been misread on certitude.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e2024.summary: Third conclusion: Christian faith is a firm certitude that is less than theology as knowledge or evidence, yet is required first, as shown from Augustine, Lombard, Dionysius and Anselm (faith seeking understanding). The corollaries: faith's adhesive certitude equals that of strict demonstration; its certitude exceeds its cognitive evidence, so theology is not merely acquired faith (against Gregory of Rimini and Gottschalk); and, against Brinkel, faith suffices by itself to inform the intellect without extrinsic evidence, otherwise unbelief would not be culpable.
claims: Faith is maximally certain but cognitively weaker than theology.
Faith is presupposed by theology.
Theology adds evidence beyond faith.
Faith alone suffices for assent without extrinsic evidence.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e2262.summary: Fourth conclusion: under the present order the truth of Christianity can be known assertively through faith or a supernatural ray (Scripture; Augustine on the need for divine aid and prior belief). Yet by divine power one can have the habit and act of faith without believing any article, since an act is separable from its actuating as an accident from its inherence (against Gregory and Gottschalk). The corollaries: baptized infants and the mentally incapable are saved without explicit belief, and one may licitly believe nothing for a time, so scriptural condemnations of unbelief concern those capable of believing.
claims: Faith or supernatural light gives assertive knowledge of Christian truth.
By God's absolute power the act of faith can exist without believing any article.
Many are saved without explicit belief.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e2412.summary: Fifth conclusion: under the present order the truth of Christianity is had adequately only through sensible signs and miracles, testimony and belief, and infused light. Against Brinkel, miracles beyond natural power compel a rational observer to acknowledge a supernatural power, as with an eclipse at full moon (with FitzRalph and Bradwardine). The corollaries: Scripture is to be relied on more than natural reason, all that is believed can be revealed within this life, and under the ordinary order no wayfarer knows Christian truth without illumination and faith. The question, as formulated, is therefore true.
claims: Miracles, testimony and infused light are the only means to Christian truth.
Miracles beyond natural power compel acknowledgment of divine action.
Under ordained power the question's thesis is true.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e123.summary: Five principal arguments against the thesis that the sincere truth of the faith requires special illumination and faith. (1) The intellect as a natural power reaches every truth, including the divine, through ens commune. (2) The damned and demons know the faith's truth without grace. (3) Special illumination can be neither coherently elevating nor assimilating. (4) Theologians do not perceive any special light and remain free to dissent. (5) Reason can demonstrate a future life, an article of faith.
claims: Natural reason suffices to know the truth of the faith.
Special illumination is incoherent or unnecessary.
Some articles of faith, such as the future life, are naturally demonstrable.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e531.summary: Five arguments for the opposite (the thesis), mostly from authority: Scripture and the Fathers on the transcendence of revealed wisdom and on all truth coming from the divine light or Holy Spirit; Augustine on wisdom being unattainable by reason alone and requiring illumination by grace; the priority of belief over understanding; and, with Scotus, the impossibility of knowing our ultimate end distinctly without revelation.
claims: Revealed wisdom exceeds human reason.
Wisdom requires illumination by God's grace.
Faith precedes understanding.
The ultimate end is known distinctly only through revelation.

jhb-l1q2-Dd1e905.summary: Division of the question: this single question will treat the whole prologue in five articles, namely opinions, definitions of terms, conclusions, objections, and replies.

jhb-l1q2a1.summary: First article: the opinions on the question, arranged as three disagreements. Among philosophers, Platonic, Avicennian and innatist views placing the principle of knowledge in some external or innate source are opposed by the Peripatetic view that locates it solely in the agent and possible intellect. Between philosophers and Christian doctors, the former affirm nature's sufficiency and the latter its need for grace and divine illumination. Among Christian theologians, Henry of Ghent and Hugolino require a special illumination distinct from the intellect, while Scotus, Thomas of Strasbourg and Gregory of Rimini deny it.
claims: Opinions divide into three disagreements.
Philosophers deny supernatural influence; Christian doctors affirm its necessity.
Theologians divide over special illumination, with Henry and Hugolino for and Scotus, Thomas of Strasbourg and Gregory against.

jhb-l1q2a2.summary: Second article: definitions of the question's key terms. 'Truth' is incomplex, complex (complexe significabile), or the true proposition. The 'Christian sect' is the congregation of the faithful under Christ. 'Reason' is the image-bearing higher soul or what naturally causes knowledge of an unknown proposition abstractively or deductively, in Hiltalingen's revised definition against Brinkel. 'Illumination' is the assisting principle, the motion, or the act. 'Faith' is an infused supernatural habit, with its canonistic equivocations, and is below science in evidence but not in certitude. The 'adherence of faith' is the wayfarer's greatest certitude, resting on revelation.
claims: Key terms are equivocal and must be distinguished.
Faith falls below science in evidence but not in certitude.
Reason is properly what naturally causes knowledge of an unknown proposition.

jhb-l1q2a3.summary: Third article: five conclusions that determine the question. (1) The Christian law binds every rational creature and condemns all error, so its truth is 'sincere'. (2) No wayfarer has perfect intuitive knowledge of any sincere truth, yet theology knows things more perfectly than other sciences by knowing them in God; sincere certitude needs the eternal exemplar, and Henry of Ghent is defended. (3) Faith is maximally certain but cognitively less than theology, which it precedes, and it suffices by itself for assent. (4) Faith or supernatural light gives assertive knowledge of Christian truth, though by absolute power faith could exist without belief in any article, and many are saved without explicit belief. (5) The truth of Christianity is had only through miracles, testimony and infused light, so under the ordinary order the question is true.
claims: The thesis of the question is true under God's ordained power.
Theology is superior in perfection of knowledge to other sciences.
Faith equals demonstration in certitude but is inferior to theology in evidence.
Miracles, testimony and infused light are the only routes to Christian truth.

jhb-l1q2a4.summary: Fourth article: objections against everything set down in articles two and three. Against the definitions: the complexe significabile reduces to things; Christ cannot be head of a Church he belongs to; the definition of the Church excludes sinners and the excommunicated; the definition of reason would include syllogistic form and the passions; illumination as the soul's art cannot be God; there are no supernatural habits or truths; faith involves fear of the opposite and is less certain than first principles. Against the conclusions: the gospel has not reached all nations; infants and the invincibly ignorant do not sin; the damned cannot keep worsening; philosophy's teaching on the eternity of the world would be error; we do know our own will intuitively; axioms give unsurpassable certitude; theology is not superior to faith (Durandus); faith's assent is free while demonstration compels; Holcot's and Brinkel's arguments that faith does not immediately cause assent; Francis of Marchia's claim that the faith is self-evident; Rome's headship; Brinkel's sensory skepticism about miracles; Albumasar's astrology; Peter's licit disbelief of Christ; and Giles's argument that clear vision necessitates love, so no wayfarer sees God clearly.
claims: Each definition and conclusion faces serious counterarguments from contemporary authors.
Skepticism about the senses and astrology challenge the evidential role of miracles.
Rationalist (Marchia) and voluntarist (Holcot, Brinkel) positions challenge the account of faith.

jhb-l1q2a5.summary: Fifth article: replies to all the objections and then to the principal arguments, with several extended digressions. Short replies defend the definitions: senses of 'truth' differ in connotation; 'Church' has several senses (with Marsilius of Padua), so Christ is both member and head; illumination is God as uncreated art; supernatural habits are 'natural' as owed but not attainable 'from nature'. On the first conclusion he distinguishes being bound by a law from being required to perform it (FitzRalph) and argues against Holcot, with Aquinas, that no true reason or science contradicts faith; Aristotle's arguments for the world's eternity reflect his own error. A long excursus on the subject and object of theology follows: God is theology's subject under the ratio of a good than which none greater can be thought, infinite equivalently rather than formally. Against Giles and Thomas of Strasbourg he argues that a theologian can have syncategorematically infinite considerations of God without comprehending him. He rejects Ockham's view that the object is the conclusion and attacks Gregory of Rimini's complexe significabile as insufficient for negative propositions and as producing absurdities about creation, annihilation and beatitude. His own semantic account holds that propositions can signify what is nothing, that the significate is what one extreme signifies (God's being is God), and that necessary, impossible and contingent propositions must be defined through equisignificant propositions. He then answers the objections on faith and theology (one theological habit; faith equal in certitude, unequal in evidence; faith plus the will suffices for assent, against Holcot and Brinkel; articles of faith rest on authority, not self-evidence), on salvation and the Roman Church, and on miracles (only infinite power could deceive the senses systematically, and Christ's knowledge of hearts and future contingents proves his divinity). He rejects astrology, explains Peter's licit disbelief, distinguishes necessity of coercion from inevitability against Giles, and finally answers the five principal arguments, holding that illumination is both elevating and assimilating and that reason cannot reach the future life as faith teaches it.
claims: No true reason or science contradicts the faith; apparent conflicts are sophisms or philosophers' errors.
God is the subject of theology under the ratio of the greatest conceivable good.
Gregory of Rimini's complexe significabile is insufficient and leads to absurdities.
The object of science is the significate of the conclusion, which can be nothing.
Faith with the will suffices for assent without extrinsic evidence.
Miracles beyond finite power give adequate grounds for faith.
Special illumination is required, both elevating and assimilating, and the question is true.

jhb-l1q2.summary: Hiltalingen's single prologue question asks whether a wayfarer can perfectly know the sincere truth of the Christian faith by human reason alone, without special divine illumination and the foundation of Catholic faith. He answers that, under God's ordained power, this is impossible. After five arguments for natural sufficiency (natural power, ens commune, the damned and demons, the incoherence of illumination, theologians' lack of any perceived light, a demonstrable future life) and five authorities for the opposite, he surveys opinions (philosophers vs. philosophers, philosophers vs. Christian doctors, Henry and Hugolino vs. Scotus, Thomas of Strasbourg and Gregory) and defines truth, the Christian sect, reason, illumination, faith and adherence. Five conclusions follow: the Christian law binds all and excludes error; no wayfarer has perfect intuitive knowledge, yet theology surpasses other sciences by knowing things in God; faith equals demonstration in certitude but is below theology in evidence and is its precondition; faith or supernatural light gives assertive knowledge, though by absolute power faith could exist without explicit belief; and Christian truth is had only through miracles, testimony and infused light. A long fourth article of objections and a fifth of replies use the question to engage contemporary debates. He argues against Holcot that faith is never contrary to reason, sets out an Augustinian (Egidian) account of God as theology's subject under the ratio of the greatest good, rejects both Ockham's and Gregory of Rimini's accounts of the object of science in favor of his own semantics of non-existent significates, defends the probative force of miracles against Brinkel's sensory skepticism, and finally holds that special illumination is both elevating and assimilating.
claims: Under the ordinary order no wayfarer can know the sincere truth of Christianity without special illumination and faith.
Theology knows more perfectly than any other created science, though no wayfarer has perfect intuitive knowledge.
Faith is as certain as demonstration but less evident than theology, and it precedes theology.
No true reason or science contradicts the faith.
Miracles, testimony and infused light are the only adequate grounds of Christian truth.
The object of science is the significate of the conclusion, not a Gregorian complexe significabile.
